#6217. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club?

#6216. How Much Do Boeing 747-8 Pilots Make In 2026?

The Boeing 747-8 is one of the largest commercial aircraft in operation. With its distinctive humpbacked fuselage, four powerful engines, and substantial payload capacity, the aircraft requires highly trained flight crews. However, the salaries these pilots receive depend more on their airline, seniority, and position than on the aircraft itself.

In 2026, Boeing 747-8 pilots can earn anywhere from six-figure annual salaries to well over $400,000, particularly at major cargo operators such as UPS Airlines. However, there is no single industry-wide salary for a 747-8 pilot, as first officers, experienced captains, and newly hired pilots work under different pay structures, with contractual guarantees and additional benefits influencing their overall compensation.

Boeing 747-8 pilot salaries vary considerably depending on the airline, years of service, and whether a pilot serves as a captain or first officer. At the upper end of the pay scale, experienced captains at major cargo airlines can earn more than $400,000 annually, while first officers typically receive lower salaries that can still reach six figures after gaining experience.

UPS Airlines offers some of the highest compensation for pilots operating the Boeing 747-8F, the freighter version of the aircraft. Under its pilot pay agreement, the top captain hourly rate reached $401 in September 2025, while the highest first officer rate reached $284. These figures provide a useful benchmark for understanding the earning potential available to experienced pilots in 2026.

Atlas Air, another major Boeing 747-8F operator, follows a different pay structure that takes account of the aircraft, pilot position, and years of service. Its 747-8F captain hourly rate starts at $247 in the first year and increases to $259 in the second year, eventually reaching $332 by the twelfth year. Consequently, the difference between an experienced captain's earnings and those of a newer pilot can be substantial.

Although salary estimates sometimes place the average US Boeing 747-8 pilot's earnings at approximately $135,000 annually in 2026, such figures need careful interpretation. Broad estimates can include junior first officers, contract pilots, and pilots working for lower-paying operators, meaning they may not accurately represent the compensation available to experienced crews at large cargo airlines.

UPS Airlines operates the Boeing 747-8F as part of its extensive cargo network, and its pilots benefit from a compensation structure negotiated with the Independent Pilots Association. The agreement includes a two-year contract extension, with the published top hourly rates providing a strong indication of what experienced pilots can earn when they reach the highest levels of seniority.

At the top of the pay scale, a UPS Boeing 747-8F captain earns $401 per hour, while a first officer earns $284 per hour, based on rates established in September 2025. Estimates put a top-rate captain's earnings at approximately $34,000 per month, equivalent to around $408,000 annually. However, actual earnings can vary according to the pilot's schedule, additional duties, and applicable contractual payments.

One important detail is that UPS Airlines does not pay its pilots according to the Boeing 747-8 alone. Its widebody pilots operate under a common pay scale covering aircraft such as the Boeing 767 and McDonnell Douglas MD-11, meaning that a captain's hourly rate is determined primarily by seniority and position rather than by the particular aircraft flown. The latest data from ch-aviation shows that UPS Airlines' fleet is currently made up of the aircraft detailed in the table above.

Newly hired UPS Airlines pilots begin considerably lower on the compensation ladder, with a probationary rate of approximately $56 to $60 per hour regardless of whether they serve as first officers or captains. This illustrates why the highest published salary should not be treated as representative of every pilot employed by the airline, particularly those who are still building seniority and experience.

Atlas Air operates the world's largest fleet of Boeing 747 freighters and is another major employer for pilots seeking to fly the aircraft. Its compensation system is negotiated through a collective agreement with Teamsters Local 2750, with hourly rates varying according to the pilot's seat, aircraft assignment, and years of service.

For Boeing 747-8 captains, the hourly rate begins at $247 in the first year, increases to $259 in the second year, and reaches $332 by the twelfth year. These rates provide a clear picture of how experience influences earnings, although the captain's annual compensation also depends on the amount of credit earned under the applicable contract and any additional payments.

Atlas Air first officers generally earn between $120,000 and $230,000 annually, while captain salaries range from approximately $250,000 to more than $450,000, according to estimates. These broad ranges reflect differences in seniority, flying schedules, and total compensation, rather than a guaranteed salary for every pilot operating a Boeing 747-8.

Atlas Air pilots have sometimes described their compensation agreement as a contract cycle behind those of major airlines that secured substantial raises after the pandemic. Nevertheless, the airline remains an important option for experienced widebody pilots, particularly those interested in international cargo operations and the opportunities that come with building seniority at a large freighter operator.

Seniority is one of the most important factors determining how much a Boeing 747-8 pilot earns in 2026. As pilots progress through an airline's pay scale, their hourly rates generally increase, allowing experienced first officers and captains to earn considerably more than colleagues who have only recently joined the company. A useful rule of thumb is to multiply the applicable hourly rate by 1,000 to estimate annual earnings.

For example, a pilot earning $284 per hour would generate approximately $284,000 using this calculation, while a captain earning $401 per hour would reach approximately $401,000. This is only a rough estimate, however, because actual pay depends on credited hours and contractual provisions.

At UPS, pilots receive a contractual guarantee of approximately 81 hours per 28-day pay period, alongside potential per diem allowances, extra compensation for certain duties, and retirement contributions. These benefits can make the overall employment package more valuable than the hourly rate alone suggests, although the exact amount depends on individual circumstances and the terms of the applicable agreement.

Mid-career Boeing 747 first officers can often earn between $180,000 and $250,000 annually, while captains at major cargo and international airlines can exceed $350,000 once additional compensation is included. Consequently, comparing salaries requires more than simply examining the published hourly rate, since guaranteed credit, seniority progression, and retirement benefits also influence the final financial outcome.

The distinction between a first officer and a captain is another major factor behind the variation in Boeing 747-8 pilot salaries. Both pilots must meet demanding training and qualification requirements, but the captain has overall authority for the flight and carries additional responsibility for operational decisions, crew coordination, and the safe conduct of the aircraft.

First officers typically occupy the lower end of the pay scale, particularly during their early years with an airline. At UPS Airlines, for example, the highest published first officer rate is $284 per hour, compared with $401 for a captain, illustrating how a pilot's position can affect earnings even when both crew members operate the same Boeing 747-8F.

Promotion to captain generally depends on experience, qualifications, available vacancies, and seniority within the airline. A pilot may accumulate substantial flight experience before securing a command position, and the timing of that promotion can significantly influence lifetime earnings. The aircraft itself does not automatically guarantee a higher salary, as the employer's pay structure remains the decisive factor. Newly hired pilots must also account for the financial realities of entering a cargo airline. Initial compensation can be considerably lower than the salaries advertised for senior captains, and probationary pay arrangements may apply before a pilot progresses through the relevant contract. Therefore, published maximum salaries describe the potential at the top of the career ladder rather than the starting point for every new employee.

The compensation available to Boeing 747-8 pilots in 2026 reflects the continued importance of experienced flight crews to large-scale cargo operations. Airlines require qualified pilots who can manage complex international flights, operate sophisticated aircraft systems, and maintain professional standards across demanding schedules, making experienced captains particularly valuable within the industry. UPS Airlines provides one of the clearest examples of the earning potential available at the top of the market, with its $401 hourly captain rate translating into an estimated annual figure of approximately $408,000 for a senior Boeing 747-8F captain. Atlas Air also offers substantial earning opportunities, although its pay progression and contract structure differ from those at UPS Airlines.

When assessing Boeing 747-8 pilot compensation and comparing it to other aircraft, the airline, the pilot's position, years of service, guaranteed flight credit, and additional benefits must all be considered together. In 2026, experienced captains at major cargo operators can earn more than $400,000 annually, while first officers and junior pilots receive lower compensation as they progress through their careers.

#6215. Ryanair Warns of Pay Freezes and Labor Unrest as Fuel Costs Surge

Photo Credit: A file photo of a Ryanair Boeing 737 Max aircraft. Ryanair

Even with a strong balance sheet, Ryanair is squeezing pay and hiring as its cheap fuel hedges run out. If the strongest airline in Europe is bracing for a difficult 2027, weaker rivals face a much harder winter.

Halloween is over, but for Europe's airlines the scariest weeks may still lie ahead. Ryanair, the continent's largest carrier, warned Monday of pay freezes, slower recruitment and AI efficiencies as it reported a 15% drop in half-year profits and braced for a €2 billion ($2.24bn) spike in its annual fuel bill in the group's fiscal 2027/28.

The low-cost giant is also anticipating potential industrial action next spring, with group CEO Michael O'Leary suggesting that a pilot strike could actually reduce costs.

"It would be helpful to us if there were strikes, I think, in April or May of next year," O'Leary told analysts on Monday's earnings call. "From a financial point of view ... in the short term, they would save us money."

The colorful commentary comes after several years of more settled labor relations, including multi-year agreements negotiated with unions across Europe. However, management appears to be taking a tougher position as those deals a

Ryanair reported a 15% drop in half-year profit after tax to €2.1 billion ($2.35bn) and warned of a €2 billion ($2.24bn) increase in its annual fuel bill in fiscal 2027/28, as the low-cost fuel hedges that have shielded it begin expiring next spring. Group CEO Michael O'Leary said covering that cost cliff through ticket prices alone would require fares to rise about 20%, or €10 per passenger, and that he doesn't expect fares to rise that far — so Ryanair will attack costs instead. The measures include pay freezes for pilot groups in Dublin, the UK, Spain, and Portugal that refuse to settle new collective agreements early, postponed pilot recruitment and training this winter, lower crewing ratios, cheaper airport deals, and greater use of AI in operations and back-office work. O'Leary told analysts that strikes in April or May would save the airline money in the short term, given fuel prices near record highs. The hard line on pay sits alongside a new €800 million ($896m) share buyback starting in February 2027, a contrast an analyst raised directly on the call. Ryanair now expects 214 million passengers in the year to March 2027, down from an earlier 216 million target, with roughly 3% growth the following year — unusually slow for a carrier targeting 300 million passengers by 2034.

#6214. Airline Passengers Are Getting Scam Emails With Real Confirmation Numbers—Some Frontier Customers Are Entering Credit Card Details

Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting emails from scammers using their real flight details and confirmation numbers, promising refunds or claiming their bookings haven’t been paid for – and telling them to enter their credit card information to complete purchases or confirm return of funds. Frontier reported an active phishing campaign targeting its customers. That doesn’t tell us where the reservation information came from. A reader sent me a refund email that claims a ticketing error caused duplicate taxes and fees and failed to apply a promotional credit. It promises a full refund after the customer confirms the original payment card. The message even supplies an explanation for why an airline that already charged you supposedly needs your card again: Because the settlement batch for this reservation has already closed, our payment system needs the original payment method confirmed so the refund can be routed back to your card. A closed settlement batch ordinarily means the merchant needs to process a refund rather than void the original transaction. In other words, it’s a made up reason meant to sound plausible. These Emails Are Using Real Reservation Details In a Frontier GoWild! Pass Holders discussion, numerous passengers say they received these emails. Several report that the confirmation numbers matched actual bookings. That includes trips already taken and travel still upcoming. One customer says the supposed refund was about five times what they’d paid. Another reports receiving both versions: a refund offer for a completed trip and a warning that payment hadn’t gone through for an upcoming reservation. A separate Reddit discussion reports the payment problem version, with an email that contained real flight information and confirmation number. Passengers report responding with their credit card numbers. One passenger says they tried several other cards before the site accepted the card originally used to book the flight. And of course a rejection message doesn’t mean the site didn’t collect the card number. Frontier Has Disclosed A Database Incident I wrote in July about a breach affecting 11,482 people. Separately, a security researcher reported that a confirmation number and last name could expose sensitive passenger information through Frontier’s systems. There’s also an October 2 notice from Frontier about a security incident involving its customer care database covering information submitted through its customer care form. They changed the database configuration and are ‘improving monitoring’. Security firm VenariX analyzed leaked samples associated with a group claiming Frontier among its victims. They found booking codes, flight numbers and dates, and evidence pointing to overly broad access permissions on Microsoft customer service portals. This Approach Has Been Used Against Hotel And Cruise Customers I’ve covered hotel scams where the sender knows the guest’s reservation details and uses them to demand payment or card verification. Knowing the hotel, dates and guest’s name makes the message much more persuasive. Norwegian Cruise Line customers reported a similar campaign in October, with messages containing real booking information and demanding payment verification. Norwegian issued its own warning. What To Do If You Received One Frontier won’t email asking you to reconfirm a reservation, re-enter card details, or supply payment information to receive a refund. Check the trip through Frontier directly. Open the app or type the airline’s website address yourself. Use contact information obtained there if something looks wrong. If you entered a card, contact its issuer. Lock it while you report the exposure and arrange a replacement. Include every card you tried, even ones the page said it rejected. Don’t assume leaving before clicking Submit protected the information. Web forms can collect what you type before submission. If you supplied a password, change it through the legitimate site. Change it elsewhere if you reused it. Check the reservation. Make sure the itinerary and contact information remain correct. Frontier’s published instructions say a confirmation code and last name can provide access to changes and cancellations, so changing your frequent flyer password may not close that separate route into a booking. Always check the sender information on an email. That can be spoofed but most scammers don’t go to that level of effort. #6213. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

Sometimes, simplicity is king. And that's certainly the case with the Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card.

The Venture Rewards is a card I frequently recommend to beginners who want to earn rewards they can maximize for travel.

Why? Because for a reasonable $95 annual fee, the card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase, making it easy to build a rewards balance without keeping track of bonus categories. Plus, it offers valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options, whether you want to keep things simple or explore more advanced strategies.

Whether you're new to earning travel rewards or recently picked up the card yourself, here are six beginner-friendly ways to make the most of the Venture Rewards.

Earning a welcome bonus is one of the easiest ways for beginners to kick-start their points and miles journey.

Currently, new Venture Rewards cardholders can earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, they'll also receive a $300 credit for Capital One Travel hotel and vacation rentals upon account opening.

According to TPG's October 2026 valuations, Capital One miles are worth 1.85 cents per mile. When including the credit, the total value of this welcome offer comes to $1,688. That makes this offer the most valuable we've seen in over two years.

Those 75,000 Capital One miles can be a great starting point for anyone new to maximizing points and miles.

And as for the $300 Capital One Travel credit, it's a great way to dip your toe into the world of travel portals. You could use it to cover a weekend hotel stay, save on a vacation rental or offset the cost of a more expensive trip.

Just remember that the credit must be used toward eligible hotel or vacation rental bookings through Capital One Travel within your first cardholder year.

Related: Credit cards 101: The beginner’s guide

One of the Venture Rewards' best perks is that it earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

With some travel rewards cards, you earn more points when spending in certain everyday categories. But with the Venture Rewards, you'll earn 2 miles per dollar whether you're filling up your tank, furnishing your apartment or stocking your fridge.

The card also earns 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through Capital One Travel.

TPG lead writer Katie Genter has held the Venture Rewards for more than a decade and still finds it useful for everyday purchases: "I like the Venture's straightforward earning structure and the fact that it earns versatile yet valuable Capital One miles."

She often uses her Venture Rewards for purchases that would earn just 1 point or mile per dollar with another rewards card.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, the Venture Rewards can be a great place to start, given how simple it is to earn rewards that can then be used for travel, which we'll cover below.

Related: The best credit cards for everyday spending

Another way to maximize your Venture Rewards as a beginner is to book eligible travel through Capital One Travel, the issuer's online travel booking platform.

As mentioned above, Venture Rewards cardholders earn 5 miles per dollar spent on hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars booked through the portal, compared to the standard 2 miles per dollar on other purchases.

For example, booking a $1,000 hotel stay through Capital One Travel would earn you 5,000 miles (compared to 2,000 miles if you booked directly with the hotel). That's an additional 3,000 miles, worth approximately $56 according to TPG's valuations.

Plus, Venture Rewards cardholders can access Capital One's Lifestyle Collection, which offers benefits such as a $50 experience credit for each eligible hotel stay and potential room upgrades (when available).

However, I don't recommend using the portal as your default method of booking travel. You usually won't earn hotel loyalty points or receive elite status benefits when booking through a third party, so it's worth comparing prices and benefits before making a reservation.

Still, for beginners looking to earn more miles without changing their spending habits, Capital One Travel can be a useful tool.

Related: Should I book flights through a travel portal?

Beyond earning miles, the Venture Rewards comes with several travel perks that can help you save money and make your trips a little easier.

One of the most useful is a statement credit of up to $120 (every four years) for a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee. All you need to do is pay the application fee with your card, and you'll receive a statement credit for the eligible charge.

Both programs can help you save time at the airport, but Global Entry also includes TSA PreCheck benefits, so I recommend it for international travelers.

Another perk for international travelers is that the Venture Rewards charges no foreign transaction fees. This means you can use your card abroad without worrying about the additional fees some credit cards charge on international purchases.

The card also offers several travel protections, including an auto rental collision damage waiver and travel accident insurance, which can provide some added peace of mind when you're away from home.

You can also enroll in complimentary Hertz Five Star status, which comes with benefits like a wider selection of rental vehicles and the ability to skip the rental counter (at certain locations).

For a card with a $95 annual fee, these perks can offer strong ongoing value, especially if you travel a few times a year.

Related: 7 of the best starter travel credit cards

If you aren't ready to transfer your miles to travel partners but still want to redeem your rewards for travel, another option is to use your miles to cover eligible travel purchases.

Rather than searching for award availability or navigating airline loyalty programs, you can book an eligible travel purchase with your card and redeem miles to offset the charge within 90 days of the purchase.

When you redeem miles this way, each mile is worth 1 cent. That's less than TPG's valuation of Capital One miles at 1.85 cents per mile, but it offers a straightforward way to use your rewards.

For example, if you book a $300 flight with your Venture Rewards, you can redeem 30,000 miles to cover the purchase. You can also use this feature for other eligible travel expenses, including hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars.

TPG director of site strategy Carly Helfand has relied on this method before, redeeming 100,000 Capital One miles to cover a last-minute Airbnb purchase.

While transferring miles to travel partners can yield higher redemption values, covering travel purchases is a useful alternative when you want to book directly or can't find award availability that works for your dates.

For potentially higher-value redemptions, consider transferring your Capital One miles to the issuer's airline and hotel partners.

If you're new to the world of travel rewards, transferring miles simply means moving your Capital One miles into another travel loyalty program, where you can then redeem them for flights or hotel stays.

Capital One has more than 15 travel partners, including Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Wyndham Rewards.

Most of Capital One's airline partners offer a 1:1 transfer ratio, meaning 1,000 Capital One miles become 1,000 miles in the partner program. However, some partners have different ratios, so be sure to check before transferring.

Personally, I love transferring my Capital One miles to airline partners to book flights to and around Europe.

For example, I recently transferred about 6,000 Capital One miles to Air France-KLM Flying Blue to book a Scandinavian Airlines flight from Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) to Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN). I paid just $11 in taxes and fees for a flight that would have otherwise cost about $450 in cash, giving me 7.3 cents per mile in value — well above TPG's valuation of 1.85 cents per mile.

If you're just getting started, don't feel like you need to master transfer partners right away. You can begin by redeeming miles for travel purchases and explore transfers as you become more comfortable.

Related: How to transfer Capital One miles to airline and hotel partners

The Capital One Venture Rewards stands out as a beginner-friendly travel rewards card thanks to its simple earning structure, valuable travel perks and flexible redemption options.

If you're new to the world of points and miles, start by using the card for everyday spending and exploring simple travel redemptions. As you become more comfortable, you can transfer miles to travel partners to unlock even greater value.

And even as you become more experienced with points and miles, the Venture Rewards' simplicity and flexibility make it a card worth keeping in your wallet long term.

For more details, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards.

Golden Week gave Thailand its first real sign that Chinese travelers were coming back. Now a single embassy advisory has put that at risk, and Lunar New Year 2027, coming in early February, will show whether the damage is a dip or something more prolonged.

Chinese arrivals to Thailand fell to 49,494 in the week of October 18–24, down about 24% from the week before, The Nation reported. Thai officials attributed the drop partly to post-holiday seasonality and partly to weaker confidence after a Chinese embassy safety warning.

Chinese arrivals to Thailand fell to 49,494 in the week of October 18–24, down about 24% from the week before, The Nation reported, with Thai officials attributing the decline partly to post-Golden Week seasonality and partly to weaker confidence after a Chinese embassy safety advisory. The October 16 advisory cited cases of Chinese nationals who went missing, were unlawfully detained, or were lured toward the Thailand–Myanmar border, and urged travelers to tighten safety precautions. Thai Hotels Association president Thienprasit Chaiyapatranun told Skift daily Chinese arrivals dropped from about 15,000 during Golden Week to about 9,000, while the Association of Thai Travel Agents said cancellations have pushed Chinese group-tour business more than 30% below last year, with a warning it could halve over Lunar New Year 2027 without government action. The reversal lands after a period of rebuilding: Minor Hotels had told Skift Chinese room nights across its Thailand portfolio were 78% ahead of last year heading into Golden Week, and China had retaken the top source market spot with about 4.2 million arrivals through October 31. Thailand has since cut its 2026 China target to 5.1 million and its full-year visitor forecast to 33 million from 36.7 million, after total foreign arrivals fell 4.1% to 24.4 million from January 1 to October 17.

#6209. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

#6208. Marriott’s Fees Jump 14% as Hotel Owners Seek a Bigger Cut

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Aerial view of The Ritz Carlton Oahu Turtle Bay. Marriott

Marriott said that its talks with hotel owners who want a bigger cut of the pie have been "constructive." It's easier for everyone to stay polite about the fee math when profit growth has revived significantly.

Marriott’s fees are climbing just as some of its hotel owners push for a bigger share of them.

Gross fees rose 14% to $1.52 billion in the third quarter, helped by a larger hotel network and by co-branded credit card fees, which Chief Financial Officer Jen Mason said on a Monday earnings call were “expected to rise in the high 30% range” for the full year. A group of owners wrote to Marriott’s management earlier this year asking for a bigger share of loyalty income, citing the card fees in particular. Net income rose 17% to $790 million.

Strong results may also give Marriott more leverage in those talks. Worldwide revenue per available room (RevPAR) rose 6.5% year over year, far above the 3.5% to 4% the company had projected in August, and Mason cited “a solid improvement in hotel margins.”

The gains reached the hotels that had been struggling most. Limited-service hotels posted a third consecutive quarter of RevPAR gains, up more than 6%.

Marriott beat expectations in the third quarter, with worldwide RevPAR up 6.5% year over year against August guidance of 3.5% to 4%, gross fees up 14% to $1.52 billion, and net income up 17% to $790 million. The company raised its full-year RevPAR outlook to 4.5% to 5%, up from the 1.5% to 2.5% it forecast in February, and offered an early view that 2027 worldwide RevPAR could grow 3.5% to 4.5%. The results land in the middle of a negotiation with a group of owners who wrote to management earlier this year asking for a bigger share of loyalty income, citing co-branded credit card fees, which CFO Jen Mason said are expected to rise in the high 30% range for the full year. CEO Anthony Capuano described Marriott's approach to owners as incremental, pointing to concessions already announced — a lower owner contribution rate on loyalty spending, better reimbursement for redemption stays on high-demand nights, relaxed operating and renovation rules, and a rebate for some well-reviewed hotels — and did not rule out more. Incentive management fees rose 22% to $181 million, which Marriott cites as evidence that owner and brand economics move together. Meanwhile, net room growth held at 4.6%, Capuano called key money the "weapon of choice" in winning development deals, and conversions made up more than a third of signings. The strong quarter arrived a week after Capuano told staff Marriott would eliminate some corporate roles while creating others; neither executives nor analysts raised the restructuring on the call.

#6207. Capital One Adds New Airline Partner With 30% Bonus—Book Emirates Business Class Without Fuel Surcharges

All of a sudden Panamanian airline Copa is taking U.S. points transfer programs by storm. Did not have that on my 2026 bingo card! Capital One has added Copa Airlines ConnectMiles as a transfer partner, opening another way to book Emirates business class without fuel surcharges. They’re offering a 30% transfer bonus to launch the partnership, too. But even with that bonus, you’ll get fewer Copa miles than Citi and Rove offer at their regular rates. Beginning November 2, Capital One miles transfer to Copa at 2:1.5. That’s 750 ConnectMiles for every 1,000 Capital One miles. The 30% bonus runs through December 1, 2026, bringing the effective rate to 975 ConnectMiles per 1,000 miles transferred. I like seeing Capital One expand its partner list again. They haven’t done so in a year! I just wish they weren’t quite so tight with the transfer ratio. Citi Added Copa Last Week, Following Rove I covered Rove adding Copa on September 1. Their regular transfer rate is 1:1, and they launched with a 40% bonus through September 30. That meant 1,000 Rove miles became 1,400 Copa miles. Then Citi added ConnectMiles on October 25: Citi Strata Elite, Strata Premier, Prestige and AT&T Access More cardholders receive 1,000 Copa miles per 1,000 ThankYou points. Other eligible ThankYou cards, including the no annual fee Citi Strata, Double Cash and Custom Cash cards, transfer 1,000 points to 700 Copa miles. Here’s how the three programs compare today: Transfer From Copa Miles Per 1,000 Points Rove 1,000 Citi, with an eligible premium card 1,000 Citi, other eligible cards 700 Capital One, regular rate 750 Capital One, with 30% bonus through December 1 975 Capital One’s bonus nearly gets you to 1:1. Transfer 10,000 Capital One miles and receive 9,750 Copa miles during the promotion. Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Copa at 3:1, with the usual 5,000-mile bonus for transferring 60,000 points. That’s 25,000 Copa miles for 60,000 Marriott points. When Rove added Copa, I liked having access to a program that the big U.S. bank currencies didn’t offer. Two months later, Citi and Capital One have followed. Rove’s 40% launch bonus is over, but their ordinary rate still beats Capital One’s promotional rate. The Value In Copa Miles Transfers Copa is a Star Alliance airline based in Panama. Its miles can book United Airlines and other alliance partners, but the redemption I flagged in September was Emirates. Emirates business class from the U.S. to Dubai for 80,000 miles one way, without carrier-imposed surcharges. Taxes and other applicable fees apply. United Airlines premium transcontinental business class for 25,000 miles one way when saver award space is available to Copa. Copa economy awards starting at 15,000 miles one way from its North America 1 region to Panama, Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northern South America. Capital One Now Has 23 Transfer Partners Capital One’s last additions were Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and I Prefer Hotel Rewards on September 23, 2025. It’s been more than a year, so it’s good to see them adding another option. Here’s the complete current list. These are the standard transfer ratios, before temporary bonuses, expressed as Capital One miles to partner miles or points. Transfer Partner Standard Ratio Aeromexico Rewards 1:1 Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Air France-KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 British Airways Club 1:1 Cathay Pacific Asia Miles 1:1 Copa Airlines ConnectMiles 2:1.5 Emirates Skywards 2:1.5 Etihad Guest 1:1 EVA Air Infinity MileageLands 2:1.5 Finnair Plus 1:1 Japan Airlines Mileage Bank 2:1.5 JetBlue TrueBlue 5:3 Qantas Frequent Flyer 1:1 Qatar Airways Privilege Club 1:1 Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer 1:1 TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go 1:1 Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 Virgin Red 1:1 Accor Live Limitless 2:1 Choice Privileges 1:1 I Prefer Hotel Rewards 1:2 Wyndham Rewards 1:1 Capital One manages the economics of its rewards program tightly. They give you 750 Japan Airlines miles per 1,000 Capital One miles, and half as many I Prefer points as Citi offers with its premium cards. Copa is another useful partner, but with a less generous conversion rate. At the regular Copa ratio, earning 2 Capital One miles per dollar on Venture X spending means earning 1.5 Copa miles per dollar. Citi Double Cash earns 2 ThankYou points per dollar on purchases as you buy and pay, and pairing it with an eligible premium ThankYou card gets you 2 Copa miles per dollar. #6206. Rosewood Beyond Sale: 30% Off Stays, Plus Rosewood Elite Perks

Luxury hotel group Rosewood has just kicked off its best sale of the year, offering savings of up to 30%, and it’s exclusively available through Rosewood Elite travel advisors. If you’ve been considering a stay at a Rosewood, this would be a great time to book.

With the Rosewood Beyond promotion, guests can save 30% off the best available rate when booking a Rosewood property through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. To cover the basics:

In order to take advantage of the Rosewood Beyond sale, you need to book through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. Ford’s team is happy to help with this, and can be reached at [email protected]. Other travel advisors are welcome to leave their contact details in the comments as well.

Let me emphasize that the 30% discount is off the best available rate, otherwise known as the flexible rate. So you couldn’t get this discount on an advance purchase rate, third or fourth night free rate, etc. So in some situations the savings here won’t be that significant, while in other cases they are huge.

While there are of course some restrictions and blackout dates, this is about as no strings attached as promotions get. The 30% off rate also offers the same flexibility as whatever the flexible rate would be, which of course varies by property.

Since the Rosewood Beyond sale is specifically being offered through Rosewood Elite travel advisors, the good news is that these reservations also unlock additional benefits, including the following:

Rosewood is a really high quality hotel brand, and you can find all the hotels here. If you’re looking for a getaway from the United States, it’s tough to beat the Rosewood Mayakoba, the Rosewood Little Dix Bay, the Rosewood Kona Village, Las Ventanas al Paraiso, etc. Rosewood also has lots of great city hotels, ranging from the Rosewood Hong Kong, to the Rosewood Sao Paulo, to The Carlyle New York.

Rosewood has brought back its biggest promotion of the year, offering 30% off the best available rate. This is valid for bookings confirmed November 3-10, 2026, and for stays through June 30, 2027.

Aside from a small list of excluded properties, this is a pretty straightforward offer that gives you the best deal you’ll find on Rosewood stays. You can even stack this with Rosewood Elite perks, to unlock breakfast, a property credit, a room upgrade, and more.

Just keep in mind that the discount is based on the flexible rate, and not based on any promotional rate you can find.

#6205. Choice Hotels Narrows Its Revenue Gap, but Its Upscale Brands Still Trail

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: The lobby of the Choice Hotels International headquarters in North Bethesda, Maryland. Choice Hotels

CEO Dom Dragisich can claim a win in budget hotels, with Choice recently outperforming the industry average. But upscale brands grew at a much lower pace than the industry averages.

Choice Hotels' budget brands outpaced their U.S. industrywide benchmark in the summer, offering an early sign of progress for CEO Dominic Dragisich. But the company's higher-priced brands continued to lag.

U.S. revenue per available room (RevPAR) grew 3.8%, roughly a 1.5 percentage points above Wall Street's forecast. Dragisich said on a Monday earnings call that October's RevPAR was about 7%.

Dragisich's core problem in August was that Choice trailed in every price tier where it competes, from economy to upscale, according to CoStar data. The third quarter improved the picture without erasing it.

"We did narrow the gap," Dragisich said, referring to Choice's performance relative to industry averages.

Choice's budget hotels outperformed the industry, growing RevPAR at 3.5% against about 2.5%, according to Truist Securities, citing CoStar data. Yet its upscale a

Choice Hotels' third-quarter results gave CEO Dominic Dragisich an early sign of progress at the low end of the portfolio and little else. U.S. RevPAR rose 3.8%, about 1.5 percentage points ahead of Wall Street's forecast, and Dragisich said October RevPAR came in around 7%. But the gains were uneven: Choice's economy brands grew RevPAR 3.5% against an industry figure of about 2.5%, while its upscale and above brands grew just 1.1% against a roughly 4% industry average, and midscale and upper-midscale grew 3.6% against about 4.5%, according to Truist Securities citing CoStar data. Truist analysts C. Patrick Scholes and Gregory Miller wrote that the result implies Choice continues to lose market share, estimating fair share would have been closer to 5% to 6% growth. The U.S. hotel sector overall grew RevPAR 7% in the quarter, according to CBRE. Choice's room count is roughly flat year over year, and Dragisich said he wants net room growth of 2% to 4%. The company took a $24 million charge to terminate an option to acquire an unnamed European hospitality business after the option "eventually migrated to an obligation" and the target's growth became more lease-based. Choice said it is prioritizing organic growth, bought RV membership club Harvest Hosts for about $130 million on October 1, and sold two owned hotels for about $34 million in net proceeds while keeping the franchise agreements, leaving 17 owned hotels.

#6204. American Airlines Philadelphia Flagship Lounge Expected To Double In Size, Taking Over The Admirals Club Next Door

American Airlines’ gorgeous Philadelphia Flagship Lounge may finally get the space it should have had from the start. Lounge staff are reportedly telling passengers it’ll take over the Admirals Club next door around March 2027, essentially doubling the size of the business class lounge before next summer’s transatlantic seasonal peak. That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose. A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door. Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me: Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year. In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected. The dimensions of the spaces are: Flagship: 12,500 square feet, with 200 seats. Admirals Club: 11,000 square feet, with 181 seats. Additional flex space: 1,364 square feet. That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint. I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services. Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too. I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA. Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week. Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important. American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship. Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well. Kennedy International AirportLos AngelesMiamiPhiladelphia+11 more More From View from the Wing

That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose.

A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door.

Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me:

Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year.

In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected.

That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint.

I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services.

Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too.

I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA.

Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week.

Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important.

American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship.

Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well.

Terrible idea. I just got the AA Executive card to use that lounge. I gave up the CSR. TheAA lounge between B and C is hospital ambiance circa 1965. It’s the old US Air lounge that hasn’t had 10 cents put into it since the merger.

Why can’t they keep the A AC open until say 3pm when the he FL rush hour begins?

It’s a great lounge with a welcoming staff. I used it several times en route to/from Europe this year. I welcome the expansion, as even in early May it was jammed by 3pm (June was even worse).

The most straightforward solution is to flex the Admirals Club space. The current setup works well before 1 p.m. Operate a separate Admirals Club and Flagship Lounge until 1 p.m., after which the Admirals Club closes and the Flagship Lounge expands to occupy the entire space until closing.

The origional plans were to have the entire space as a Flagship lounge prior to the pandemic. Maybe take over the old BA club and old Adirmals A club (because let’s face it that was over crowded too) and give A east and west proper clubs. Now can they do something about the clubs in PHX!!!!

I was there two weeks ago before my flight to AMS. It was PACKED in the early evening. Many people after me were not able to find a place to sit. As a side note, I tried the Philly Cheesesteak Sandwich…NOT worth repeating.

I’ll be canceling my AA Executive card if this happens without a suitable replacement.

Beyond welcome bonuses, points and miles aren't always the easiest to earn. That's why I advocate for stacking your card's earning rates with shopping portal bonuses and other promotions whenever you can.

That's exactly what I did recently when I purchased three tickets for my parents and me to see the Portland Timbers while they were visiting. The total charge was about $180; if I’d paid with a card earning just 1 point per dollar spent and skipped the other offers, I’d have earned only 180 points.

But by paying close attention to my Chase Freedom Flex®'s (see rates and fees) quarterly categories and promotions offered by Rove and Paze, I was able to walk away with just shy of 4,000 points (or over $75 in value back). Here's exactly how my earnings break down.

For Q3 2026, the Freedom Flex offered select live entertainment as one of its rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories (activation required; on up to $1,500 in combined quarterly category spending per quarter).

Despite being marketed as a cash-back card, the Freedom Flex actually earns Ultimate Rewards points. That means my earning rate for live entertainment purchases in Q3 was effectively 5 points per dollar spent, since I have an eligible card that allows me to convert my Freedom Flex rewards into fully transferable points.

On its own, this category earned me about 900 points, a solid haul considering I'd earn only 180 points during quarters when live entertainment isn't offered. Still, while planning my purchase, I knew I could do better.

I've been a big fan of Rove over the past several months, using it for a variety of events and travel bookings. Rove offers members the opportunity to earn Rove miles, which are transferable to over 20 airline and hotel partners. This includes partners that aren't offered by any credit card loyalty programs, such as Frontier Miles and Lufthansa Miles & More.

It's free to join. Rove has its own travel booking portal, but for this particular purchase, I focused solely on its shopping portal. At the time, Rove offered 6.5 miles per dollar spent on StubHub purchases.

By booking my tickets through StubHub, I earned over 1,100 Rove miles. An unfortunate downside to shopping through Rove is that your miles often take an extended amount of time to post, which isn't uncommon with shopping portals. I'm still waiting for my miles to land in my account, which Rove indicates could take until early December.

Don't forget to start your purchase in the Rove app, on Rove's website or via its browser extension. If you're using the browser extension or accessing Rove via desktop, make sure all other shopping portal browser extensions are disabled.

With my decision to book through StubHub, there was one more way I could make my purchase work for me: Paze.

Currently, eligible Chase cardholders can earn 10 additional Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent when checking out with Paze at select merchants (through Dec. 31). StubHub is among those eligible for this promotion, meaning I could triple-dip on my purchase.

Checking out with Paze instead of the standard StubHub checkout process earned me roughly 1,800 additional points.

Using Paze at checkout is easy. You should be able to select it as a payment method on your eligible merchant's checkout screen, just as you would with a digital wallet or credit card.

One technical snag to note: I wasn't able to get Paze to work on mobile, but it worked on the first try on desktop. My transaction didn't say anything about Paze, so don't fret if the same is true for you. My points posted with no problem after a few days, but I recommend screen recording your purchase as proof if you're worried.

To summarize, here's how my earnings and their value broke down in the end:

*Valuations are according to TPG's November 2026 valuations and are not provided by credit card or program issuers.

My Freedom Flex is one of my oldest cards, but I still pull it out regularly, thanks in large part to strategies like this. While Chase's Paze promotion isn't limited to this card, the Freedom Flex is the only Chase card currently open to applicants that offers rotating 5% quarterly bonus categories.

Live entertainment reliably appears as a quarterly category every year, so I expect I'll be able to replicate this strategy (or a similar one) in 2027.

The more credit cards you open, the harder it becomes to find new welcome bonuses to earn. With welcome offers being the main way to earn heaps of rewards at once, it's important to have other ways to earn points and miles when that well starts to dry up.

Knowing how to maximize your purchases, especially larger ones or those you're splitting with friends or family, will help you maintain a large rewards balance even when you're not actively applying for new credit cards.

If you're currently not a Freedom Flex cardholder, you can apply and, upon approval, have the chance to earn $250 cash back (or 25,000 bonus points) after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. That's one of the easiest welcome bonuses to earn right now, but this offer ends soon.

If you hold an eligible Ultimate Rewards card, such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see ), you can transfer the points you earn with your Freedom Flex to Chase's 14 transfer partners.

The Timbers weren't able to walk away with the win, but the more than 3,800 points and miles I earned from the tickets I purchased helped ease the sting of that loss.

You can create a strategy like this with virtually any card in your wallet. Consider the offers, limited-time earning rates and promotions that are available for your specific card; take a look at shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove to see what they offer; and use sites like Cashback Monitor to make sure you're getting the best deal.

Effectively maximizing your card's earning potential means thoroughly understanding which offers and deals are available to you and knowing how to combine them. It requires a little extra work on your part, but that effort will be worth it when those extra rewards help take you on your next dream trip.

#6201. Skift Commerce Summit 2026: Five Decisions in the Room

AI agents are here. Travel isn’t ready. Decisions made today will determine who controls the booking, the customer relationship, and the economics of travel commerce.

AI agents are already booking travel. One invite-only booking agent reported more than $1 billion a year in transaction volume, half of which was travel. Investors have already placed their bets on who wins and who loses. Most travel companies are still built for a traveler who searches, scrolls, and clicks.

Direct or third-party distribution used to be the primary choice travel suppliers had to make. Now an agent may decide which brands show up, which system can complete the booking, which card pays, and which loyalty program earns. Hotels alone spend more than $105 billion a year on distribution, and AI companies want a share of it.

The agents are here. Travel is not ready. Travel companies have to connect the dots inside the new travel commerce stack, and Skift Commerce Summit brings senior commerce leaders together around five decisions travel companies have to make now.

Operator Ticket $275 · for the people who run commerce at travel companies. Vendor Ticket $1,500 · capped, limited supply. Group rates: events@skift.com

AI has moved quickly into the travel customer journey for inspiration and planning, but not booking… yet. According to Skift Research, direct suppliers lead with a 49% net comfort score, followed by packaged tours at 37%, travel agents at 34%, loyalty portals at 31%, and OTAs at 20%. AI and chatbots score -7%. [1]

However, Skift Research describes the discovery path shifting from “search-scroll-compare” toward “ask-shortlist-decide.” As soon as travelers gain confidence in booking through AI platforms, space for brands “on the shelf” is poised to shrink. [2]

Hotels, airlines, or other travel retailers are racing to optimize for AI discoverability, but the more control they give to AI platforms, the more they risk losing direct customer relationships. They have to decide how to prioritize what they value most, and whether distribution alone is worth it if they become interchangeable within someone else’s interface.

Travelers are comfortable booking across a wide range of channels, but that also means today’s marketplace has a wider swath of competitors.

Travel’s AI discussion is moving downstream. It’s not only a customer relationship question, but also a technological one. Even if they’re discovered, booked, and integrated into the loyalty ecosystem, brands have to ensure the infrastructure works when an AI agent starts to handle trip management.

It’s one thing for an AI assistant to drive traffic to a brand’s site. The open decision is whether travel companies find it worthwhile to give an agent the tools to compare offers, change or cancel an order, and fix problems on the traveler’s behalf.

A better conversational front end can’t compensate for fragmented inventory, legacy servicing systems, or commerce technology designed for humans.

Banks, card issuers, retailers, membership programs, and technology platforms have built businesses around the traveler without having to own (or even sell) an airline seat or hotel room. They can make money from payments, rewards, subscriptions, advertising, financing, and the broader customer relationship surrounding a trip.

That changes the competitive economics for travel companies. A bank can use travel to increase card spend. A membership business can use it to make a subscription more valuable. A technology platform can influence the purchase while monetizing the customer elsewhere. These companies can compete for the same traveler without depending on the booking itself for most of their economics.

The decision is how much of that value suppliers and other travel-native companies can capture themselves as more of the commercial relationship moves into ecosystems built outside the industry.

Non-travel companies are profiting more and more off travel, stepping in to sell ancillaries and earn loyalty. 32% of travelers rank credit-card or bank loyalty programs as the most rewarding, ahead of hotel programs at 26% and airline programs at 20%. [1]

The direct-versus-third-party debate has shaped travel distribution strategy for decades. The economics have never been as simple as choosing one side. A direct booking can carry marketing, loyalty, technology, and acquisition costs of its own. An intermediary can bring incremental demand, reach a customer the brand would not have acquired directly, or fill inventory that otherwise would have gone unsold.

The channel mix is also getting more crowded. OTAs remain important, but banks, credit-card programs, membership platforms, social channels, AI interfaces, and other partners are creating new paths to the customer. Each comes with different costs, different access to customer data, and a different ability to generate demand.

The decision is which channels produce the strongest return for a particular customer, market, and trip. The best distribution strategy may use direct channels to deepen valuable customer relationships while paying intermediaries when they can deliver demand more efficiently than the brand can acquire it on its own.

“The competition to be a travel distributor has never been this intense,” says Skift Research, pointing to credit cards, social platforms, AI-native tools, OTAs, and suppliers all competing for a larger role in the booking journey. [3]

Travel companies can find unique growth opportunities by leveraging an existing customer base, brand, asset, or operating capability to create a new revenue stream. The challenge occurs when they find themselves wading into businesses they were not originally built to run.

The decision is how far that expansion should go. Some adjacencies strengthen the core business because they use capabilities the company already has. Others require new technology, operations, capital, or customer behavior that the company has never had to manage before. Growth can create leverage. It can also create complexity faster than revenue.

A Skift and ZS survey found that 75% of senior travel executives have non-core assets they can monetize, but only 32% described their current approach to doing so as “very” innovative. [4]

Discovery no longer guarantees ownership. Distribution extends beyond an OTA or supplier website and, indeed, beyond travel-native companies themselves. Payments and loyalty can generate value beyond the booking. AI is becoming another intermediary, another channel, and eventually the buyer itself.

Every travel company now faces the same question: which parts of the customer relationship, the transaction and the economics do you need to own before an agent stands between you and the traveler, and which can sit on someone else’s platform?

The Skift Commerce Summit is built to help you answer it, and to show you where your company is least ready.

Decision intelligence for travel leaders.
