#6087. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6084. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout in “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which his to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way in to the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for the fact he reveals of his subjects’ prejudices.

But then, they never were. The laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, such have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as the turn where Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, staring with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach, it is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. However, if there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6081. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.

World Brief: The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea during her annual State of the European Union address.

“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said while standing beside Carney. “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well.” Canadian officials applauded the proposal, with Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador to the EU, saying at the time that Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc.

Yet a statement prepared for this week’s annual Canada-EU summit included a watered-down version of such a future. Rather than explicitly noting the proposed associate member status, the draft text offered “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” Politico reported on Wednesday. According to Reuters, a previous draft had included at least two direct mentions of Canada’s associate member status while adding that defining the term would take another year.

“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said on Thursday. She described this type of relationship as open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together,” and she stressed that associate member status is not fully off the table.

Von der Leyen’s decision to back off from her full-throated appeal for associate Canadian membership may have been made due to some member nations’ hesitance. Several EU countries, particularly Germany, had argued that they would not approve such a designation, as it had no legal precedent and had not been fully fleshed out. Others accused von der Leyen of not discussing the idea with European leaders first.

“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” one diplomat told the Guardian. “This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying.”

The EU’s move to soften the language is likely to appease at least one foreign leader: U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump had called the EU’s initial proposal “laughable” and warned that such a designation could be considered a “hostile act” that could prompt the White House to cut off trade with Europe in certain areas. Already, U.S. trade relations with Canada and the European Union are greatly strained, with Trump repeatedly returning to his tariff war for economic leverage.

Still, Carney appeared to be unconcerned by Thursday’s language shift. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”

Who will run the ECB next? European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will step down from her role in February, officially triggering a race to determine who will take up the mantle of one of the European Union’s top posts. Her eight-year term was set to end in October 2027; her early departure allows the EU to choose her successor before one of its members, France, holds a consequential presidential election that could upset the bloc’s balance.

In April, France will hold a highly anticipated presidential vote that could see far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen take power. Eurozone members had worried that a Le Pen victory could affect who is selected to be the new ECB president, as the populist lawmaker has previously criticized EU financial institutions and expressed disinterest in choosing another mainstream central banker to lead the body. Lagarde resigning early therefore allows outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron to have a say in her replacement instead.

Among the front-runners for Lagarde’s post are former Spanish Central Bank head Pablo Hernández de Cos and former Dutch Central Bank chief Klaas Knot. Whoever is chosen will have to contend with energy price shocks, bond market turmoil, and persistent high inflation.

Meanwhile, it is unclear what’s next for Lagarde, who was the first woman to serve as the ECB president. “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” Lagarde said on Thursday. Some analysts believe that Lagarde, who is a French citizen, aims to become more vocal in the country’s politics, which have faced weeks of upheaval due to sweeping student-led protests.

Xi’s latest purge. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) confirmed the expulsion of 33 senior political and military officials on Thursday, in one of President Xi Jinping’s most sweeping purges since taking office in 2012. Those removed include Liu Jianchao, the former head of the CCP’s International Department; former Politburo member Ma Xingrui; Zhang Youxia, once the country’s most senior general; and Zhong Shaojun, a top military secretary to Xi.

It is unclear what charges these members faced beyond “serious disciplinary and legal violations.” But the expulsions are part of Xi’s extensive anti-corruption campaign targeting those considered disloyal to the party, and it comes as the longtime leader is preparing to clinch a fourth term in office. “While maintaining a tough stance against corruption, we should also strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power,” read a communiqué released by the CCP’s Central Committee on Thursday.

The announcement concluded this year’s multiday Central Committee meeting in Beijing. Only 279 officials attended the annual conference, compared to 376 members when the current body was formed in 2022. This was the first time during Xi’s term that the plenary’s attendance dropped below 300 people. That suggests that nearly 100 officials were likely purged from the party over the course of just four years, China experts say.

National mourning. Spanish search-and-rescue operations stretched into Thursday following a deadly high-speed train crash the day before. At least 69 deaths have been confirmed thus far, with some 50 individuals still hospitalized, and local authorities fear that the death toll could rise. Madrid declared three days of national mourning starting Thursday.

Early Wednesday, a high-speed passenger train believed to be going around 120 miles per hour slammed into a stopped train near the central Spanish city of Toledo. An initial investigation found that an information technology failure involving railroad switching equipment was to blame. However, critics have accused the Spanish government of failing to provide adequate oversight and maintenance of the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, particularly after another train crash on the same line killed 46 people in January.

“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Wednesday. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.” With the country holding snap parliamentary elections next month, public transportation reform will likely be a top concern among voters.

The Vatican Museums opened a new exhibition on Thursday that celebrates more than 100 years of papal travel. Dubbed “A Century of the Popemobile,” the showing features eight Mercedes-Benz vehicles that popes have used since 1930 to travel among the faithful. Notable design alterations include Pope John XXIII’s 300 d Landaulet, which included removable rear side windows to allow the pontiff to reach out to those he passed on the road, and Pope John Paul II’s 230 G, which added the car’s transparent dome for greater viewing access.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Saudi Arabia compares the Houthis to the Islamic State, Riyadh considers UAE reconciliation amid the Yemen war, and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s post-midterms impeachment risk.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Situation Report. John is once again flying solo for this edition, but Rishi will be back in action next week!

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Saudi Arabia compares the Houthis to the Islamic State, Riyadh considers UAE reconciliation amid the Yemen war, and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s post-midterms impeachment risk.

The Houthis are causing major problems for Saudi Arabia. The Iran-backed militants made significant territorial gains along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline in September, and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government is struggling to push the Houthis back. Meanwhile, the group has launched deadly strikes in Saudi Arabia that have disrupted air travel and damaged key energy infrastructure.

Riyadh is pushing for more international support as the conflict escalates. In a New York Times op-ed this week, the Saudi ambassador to the United States, Reema Bandar al-Saud, compared the Houthis to the Islamic State, saying that the Yemeni group is “underestimated” in the same way that the Islamic State was before it declared a caliphate.

She urged the international community to “set a clear goal to end the Houthis as an armed terrorist force,” arguing that the Islamic State “was defeated by local forces backed by a coalition of more than 80 nations. The Houthis can be defeated the same way.”

Defining the threat. Unlike the Islamic State, the Houthis do not seek to establish a global Islamic caliphate. Their objectives are less ambitious and are centered on conquering Yemen and removing Saudi influence from the country.

But there’s no doubt that the Houthis pose a significant regional threat. Their asymmetrical tactics, including the use of low-cost drones, have proved to be a serious challenge even for a wealthy country with a sophisticated military like Saudi Arabia. And with Israel having severely degraded the capabilities of Hamas and Hezbollah over the last several years, the Houthis are now one of the most powerful Iranian proxies in the Middle East. In addition to attacking Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have also targeted Israel with strikes, including this year, and in 2022 attacked Abu Dhabi.

The problems the Houthis cause also have global implications—particularly their attacks on shipping in the Red Sea. Their recent territorial gains have given them more control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and have led to a dual-chokepoint crisis as the Iran war has simultaneously impacted traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. There’s also evidence of Houthi collaboration with other terrorist groups in the region, including al-Shabab, an al Qaeda affiliate in Somalia.

“The Houthi threat is not only to Yemenis. We have seen that it’s a threat to Yemen, of course, but also to the region and to the international community,” said Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political advisor to Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba. “This is not a local threat. It’s a threat for everyone.”

International involvement. Though some countries have offered Riyadh increased defensive assistance—such as the United Kingdom, Egypt, Pakistan, and Turkey—there’s been a general reluctance to get directly involved on the ground. Most critically, the United States, which has conducted strikes on the Houthis in the past (including last year), has so far avoided directly intervening this time around.

The internationally recognized Yemeni government is also calling for increased international involvement, but not necessarily intervention in Yemen itself.

“We’re not asking for any boots on the ground,” Noman said. “We’re not asking for people to come to fight on our behalf.” This is “our fight,” and “we have the forces,” Noman said.

What is needed from the international community is humanitarian assistance, Noman said (read more on the humanitarian crisis in Yemen here). Riyadh and the Yemeni government are also pushing more countries to follow Washington’s example and designate the Houthis as a terrorist group to help isolate the group financially. The Yemeni government has also asked the United States for training and intelligence support.

“We’re fighting on behalf of others as well” due to the broader threat posed by the Houthis, Noman added. “That’s why we need the support from our friends and allies.”

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has axed yet another top military official, adding to a long list of firings since he became Pentagon chief. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia has been removed from his role as director of strategy, plans, and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Sylvia was removed for allegedly leaking classified information to the press, a Pentagon official told ABC News.

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

The missing link in Yemen? Riyadh and Abu Dhabi reconciling could be a game-changer in the fight against the Houthis, a top expert on Yemen told John this week. Read more here to find out why the United Arab Emirates could help turn the tide.

Impeaching Hegseth. Hegseth could face impeachment if Democrats win big in next week’s midterm elections. FP’s Rachel Oswald interviewed Democratic Rep. Mike Levin about his support for impeaching the Pentagon chief, and the legal and political considerations. Read it here.

Friday, Oct. 30: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is poised to host the G-20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia.

Tuesday, Nov. 3: The United States is set to hold midterm elections.

#6074. Trump’s closing midterm argument, Reflecting Pool edition

President Donald Trump on Monday delivered an unconventional midterms closing argument after spending weeks dropping comments at rallies aimed at sowing doubts about the election — and what he might do to contest races Republicans lose.

After barnstorming states with competitive Senate races the last few weeks, Trump delivered his final message in Washington, D.C. He even chose the Reflecting Pool by the Lincoln Memorial — the site of a refurbishment he oversaw that was plagued by questionable work that continues to reverberate politically and legally.

There had been rumblings online last week that he would be in Michigan to close out his rally blitz alongside former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers, who is in a Toss-up race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. That race was rocked Sunday when Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost a primary to El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican nominee. Alas, Trump chose the nation’s capital and mused about pool liner colors, an issue that has not overtaken voter concerns about the cost of living, corruption, the Iran war and other issues, according to public polling.

“We resurfaced the bottom in a beautiful dark blue, very dark blue. They call it ‘American flag blue,’ but it’s very dark,” he said, wearing a suit, tie and white baseball cap. “And if you had a regular blue, like I personally love the lighter color blue, but then you wouldn’t have any reflectors.”

He also plugged his proposed arch, made questionable statements about crime rates and boasted about his other Washington, D.C., fountain and park projects. He did not mention Tuesday’s election —which he deemed “the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime” — until after the 22-minute mark. Once he moved on from boasting about his D.C. projects, Trump touted his second administration’s policy record. And himself.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime. The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history,” he said. “These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He noted he had held 29 rallies in recent weeks. He contended Iran’s military platforms and stockpiles were “way down.” He touted statistics about the economy.

“Personal incomes are the highest in history. The poverty rate is at an all-time record low,” he said, adding. “American exports are at an all-time high, and more people are working today than at any point in the history of our country. And the United States is now by far the largest supplier of oil and natural gas anywhere in the world.”

The Reflecting Pool event came after he spent weeks on the campaign trail making warnings about elections — specifically, ones Democrats have won and might win this week.

For instance, during an Oct. 20 campaign rally in North Carolina for former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, Trump returned to casting doubt on his 2020 loss.

“What a lot of people don’t know is that we got screwed in 2020,” Trump said that evening, referring to the presidential race he lost to Joe Biden. “We did great. But you know who … didn’t allow it to happen was Michael Whatley. We were winning everything. You went to bed [at] 10:00. The race was over.

“Then all of a sudden, Georgia happened and some other things happened. Pennsylvania happened,” he said, continuing to cast doubt on his losses that year in both states despite no evidence of fraud.

“But we can’t forget,” he told loyalists in eastern North Carolina. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales lists the race as leaning toward Cooper.

Trump also offered the same crowd a preview of what his administration and political organizations have signaled for Tuesday at strategically selected polling stations with competitive House and Senate races.

“You know what didn’t happen? North Carolina didn’t happen,” he said to cheers about the 2020 election. “Because he had 619 lawyers at every station watching, watching, watching.”

Democratic lawmakers and pro-voter groups have warned for months that they fear pro-Trump election monitors — or even federal agents — could try to intimidate anti-Trump voters from casting ballots. Some sources have even raised concerns the administration might try seizing ballots in places that could swing a close outcome toward Republican candidates.

Trump’s rally rhetoric also suggests he will raise doubts not just about the outcomes the votes produce, but how they were cast.

“The whole thing is corrupt,” he told rallygoers Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa. “Go to paper ballots, everybody. Nice, beautiful paper ballots. You know, the paper ballots cost 9 percent of what these crooked machines cost, so you’d save a lot,” he said, without offering evidence that electronically cast ballots are problematic.

He even set the stage for casting doubt over or challenging Democratic-won races in states with GOP chiefs executive.

“And even Republican governors, many of them, they, they just do it,” he said of using voting machines over watermarked paper ballots. “I don’t know, it’s hard to believe. But you go to paper and you have the ballot there, and it’s so simple, and they put it in stacks.”

Still, Trump and his team have questioned the counting of paper ballots before — in 2020 in places like Arizona, Georgia and Pennsylvania, but to no avail. That didn’t stop him on Sunday, like at previous campaign stops, from alleging Democrats would still try shenanigans.

“It’s, look, they’ll try figuring something [out], but it’s much harder, because they have to cheat,” he said without providing evidence. “Because without, look, their policies are so bad.”

One GOP strategist, granted anonymity to be candid, said it was “normal” for any party to contest “some” election results.

Former Pennsylvania GOP Rep. Charlie Dent on Friday said Trump’s rally rhetoric appears mostly aimed at influencing public opinion and could be lacking a legitimate legal strategy.

“I’m not sure how he would intend to make a challenge to the certification of some members who may win by comfortable margins,” Dent said. “There might be circumstances where you have some contested outcomes shortly after the election that are very close. But then you’ll have a legal process and a recount process to go through to ultimately determine who the winner is.

“But once those winners are determined and the states certify those elections, then everything that’s done or said in Washington is merely ministerial at that point,” he added. “If there are objections to a particular outcome, there are legal remedies candidates can seek out.”

Mark Zaid, an attorney who has sued the Trump administration multiple times, said Monday that “the danger with his rhetoric is that he expects people to react to what he says and implement his words into action.

“He did that on Jan. 6 and he continues to do it now,” Zaid added, referring to the January 2021 Capitol riot by a pro-Trump mob following his fiery Ellipse speech that morning raising doubts about his loss to Biden.

“My own view is that post-Nov. 3 he will act far more like a cornered animal, more dangerous than when an avenue of escape is available — and implement a scorched-earth response to anything that is thrown at him,” he added. “I find it amazing that his rhetoric seemingly goes unchallenged by his base.”

Trump appeared in a relaxed mood on Monday, joking that he intended to rename the Reflecting Pool to include his name.

“I’m only kidding,” he said, looking toward assembled media members. “Please, don’t report it.” Later, about the midterms, he said the party of sitting presidents typically loses, adding matter-of-factly: “We gave this a very strong shot.”

#6072. Russia’s Next Mobilization Is Already Happening

Analysis: Russia’s Next Mobilization Is Already Happening

Understanding the conflict four years on.

Nothing in almost five years of Russia’s war on Ukraine did more damage to the Kremlin’s hold on Russian public opinion than when Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree to forcibly mobilize 300,000 men for the war on Sept. 21, 2022. Levada’s monthly mood survey, run continuously since the 1990s, recorded the sharpest one-time collapse in its history: The share of Russians describing their general mood as “great” fell from 15 percent to 7 percent almost overnight, while those reporting fear more than tripled. The share who believed the war was “progressing successfully” dropped from 73 percent in May to 53 percent by the end of September. An estimated 300,000 to half a million men of fighting age left the country within two weeks of the decree, more than had fled during all of the war up to then. Kazakhstan alone recorded some 400,000 arrivals from Russia by late November that year. At the Verkhny Lars border crossing into Georgia, cars were lined up for days.

So acute was the fallout from the 2022 mobilization drive that many concluded it was too risky for Putin to repeat—even in an authoritarian police state where citizens’ opinions matter little. Thus, the biggest question surrounding Russia’s sham parliamentary elections last month was never who would win, but whether another extremely unpopular mobilization would have to wait until after the vote.

Nothing in almost five years of Russia’s war on Ukraine did more damage to the Kremlin’s hold on Russian public opinion than when Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree to forcibly mobilize 300,000 men for the war on Sept. 21, 2022. Levada’s monthly mood survey, run continuously since the 1990s, recorded the sharpest one-time collapse in its history: The share of Russians describing their general mood as “great” fell from 15 percent to 7 percent almost overnight, while those reporting fear more than tripled. The share who believed the war was “progressing successfully” dropped from 73 percent in May to 53 percent by the end of September. An estimated 300,000 to half a million men of fighting age left the country within two weeks of the decree, more than had fled during all of the war up to then. Kazakhstan alone recorded some 400,000 arrivals from Russia by late November that year. At the Verkhny Lars border crossing into Georgia, cars were lined up for days.

So acute was the fallout from the 2022 mobilization drive that many concluded it was too risky for Putin to repeat—even in an authoritarian police state where citizens’ opinions matter little. Thus, the biggest question surrounding Russia’s sham parliamentary elections last month was never who would win, but whether another extremely unpopular mobilization would have to wait until after the vote.

The election itself was depressingly predictable. Putin’s party, United Russia, won roughly 58 percent and 349 of 450 seats, its largest majority ever. The other parties are all Kremlin-approved, with true opposition parties quickly banned. Kremlin insiders told Meduza that participation in this sham was secured “through very dirty means”: state employees ordered to report their own votes, teachers made to track which parents had voted and report every two hours, managers calling out nonvoters in group chats.

More than five weeks later, there is no mobilization decree. The Kremlin, of course, has been denying any such plan all along—18 times in the three months before the vote, according to the Moscow Times’ count. On Sept. 1, Putin called the rumors “chush sobachya” (roughly, “dogshit”) and an “information attack.” Two days later, he said: “There is no scenario today that would require mobilization.”

As Russia observers like to scoff, something isn’t true until the Kremlin denies it. Two days before Putin’s 2022 mobilization decree, then-Duma Defense Committee chair Andrey Kartapolov assured Russians they had no reason to fear that such a thing might happen. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also issued a high-profile denial just before it was announced.

This time around, however, asking whether there will be another mobilization decree may be asking the wrong question. That nothing has been announced does not mean that a new mobilization wave is not happening. Those expecting a grand announcement followed by another stampede to the border will probably be disappointed—because there is no need for another decree.

For one, the old mobilization never quite ended. In May 2023, the Russian Supreme Court ruled that a mobilization period runs from the day it is declared until a decree formally ends it. No such end-of-mobilization decree exists, and the state keeps legislating on that basis. In July, for example, parliament expanded the pool of convicts eligible for military service in a law that explicitly applies “during mobilization, martial law, or wartime.” In August, a Supreme Court ruling mentioned “the period of mobilization” as an aggravating circumstance when it upheld a five-year sentence against a Chita man convicted over a comment on social media. Legally, Russia has been continuously mobilized since 2022. Nothing requires Putin to sign anything new.

Nor is the Kremlin desperate enough for manpower to abandon the methods that have worked so far: financial inducements and ad hoc coercion instead of a dramatic nationwide call-up. Even as Ukraine now imposes around 30,000 to as many as 40,000 casualties on the Russians each month, recruitment is strained but not breaking. According to Janis Kluge, who tracks Russian recruitment numbers by looking at regional budget payments, about 263,000 new contracts were signed in the first nine months of 2026, down from 292,000 during the same period last year, with September running at roughly 1,000 a day. The average sign-up bonus has climbed to almost 2 million rubles (or almost $25,000) per contract, nearly 30 percent more than last year. In the Khanty-Mansi region of Siberia, for example, the one-time sign-up bonus is roughly 30 times the average local monthly wage.

With recruitment struggling to replace battlefield losses, the authorities have increasingly resorted to force. Since June, independent Russian outlets have documented draft raids where plainclothes men in unmarked vans, sometimes with regional government license plates, grab men off the street or out of workplaces and take them to enlistment offices to sign contracts under duress. By late August, three legal-aid groups told Verstka that they had complaints from at least 17 regions. Idite Lesom, a hotline for draft dodgers, took three times as many calls in August as during the same month one year earlier. Its director, Grigory Sverdlin, describes who gets targeted in the recruitment raids: men, largely in poor, remote regions, who are burdened with debt, under police investigation, or facing other exploitable circumstances.

There is a long history of foreigners idealizing Russia and exaggerating its power.

In Nizhny Tagil, authorities reportedly paid private “recruiters” 400,000 rubles per man delivered, and a local prosecutor has complained that violent gangs and corrupt police have joined the trade. Kluge told CNN that coercion of this kind is probably not directed from Moscow, which only sets recruitment quotas for each region to fulfill. Passing responsibility down to governors, employers, and private agents—and not asking questions about how the targets are met—keeps the Kremlin, and in particular Putin, from being associated with the abuses.

The line between regular conscripts—young draftees who normally don’t serve in war—and the contract soldiers who do is also blurring. Since January, Russia has run a perpetual draft, with call-ups year-round and dispatches to units each spring and fall. The General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces said about 120,000 conscripts from the fall cycle began heading to their units on Oct. 10, allegedly none posted to Ukraine. But Putin has repeatedly pledged not to send conscripts or reservists to fight. Only six months after Putin first made that pledge in March 2022, the reservists were called up. Similarly, conscripts barely out of bootcamp were dispatched to repel the Ukrainian incursion into Russia’s Kursk region in August 2024, where many died or were captured.

That teenage or 20-something conscripts aren’t sent to fight and die in Ukraine remains technically true while missing the point, since they are routinely pressured into signing contracts. These contracts are then effectively indefinite due to the 2022 mobilization decree, still active, that makes it all but impossible for them to quit. Their coerced signature on a contract, in other words, removes the distinction that Putin’s pledge to young conscripts and their families relies on. Idite Lesom logged dozens of appeals in August from conscripts (and their relatives) facing persuasion, threats, or worse.

The population targeted by the ongoing mobilization has barely changed since 2022. At that time, the men were disproportionately drawn from non-ethnic-Russian republics such as Buryatia, Dagestan, Tuva, and Yakutia, where poverty, high unemployment, low salaries, few alternatives, and a sign-up bonus made military service a relatively attractive option. The women-led protests against the war that followed were concentrated there as well, as were the harshest crackdowns. The current wave of draft raids has followed a similar pattern so far. It is concentrated in poor, remote, and administratively sidelined places like Penza and Izhevsk, although draft-age men are now also being stopped in the streets of Moscow.

None of this proves that a formal call-up won’t come. If the situation at the front deteriorates sharply or recruitment numbers plummet, Putin could sign a new decree. But that would be a public admission that the quiet system has failed, and any nationwide announcement would bring back the shock—and potential exodus—of September 2022. Until then, Russia will keep feeding its war machine as it does now: With a recruiter intent on meeting his quota and getting his cut, snatching men into an unmarked van with tinted windows in a crumbling post-industrial town thousands of miles from Moscow.

Alexey Kovalev is an independent journalist and former investigations editor at Meduza who left Russia in 2022. X: @Alexey__Kovalev
