#6065. 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign

Republicans began the 2026 election cycle on a high, with a governing trifecta in Washington and heavy optimism that the coalition that swept Donald Trump back into the White House represented a durable new voting bloc. They had a favorable Senate map and insisted there were opportunities to expand their narrow House majority.

But Trump’s policies, economic anxieties, historical trends and an unpopular war have upended  the calculus for the midterm elections. At the close of the campaign, the fight for Congress is taking place mostly on Republican turf, a striking shift in less than two years.

Here are 15 moments that shaped the 2026 midterm campaign:

Less than three months after taking office, Trump made good on a campaign promise: a 10 percent minimum tariff on all imports and higher duties on nations that run trade surpluses with the U.S. Since proclaiming “Liberation Day,” the on-and-off tariffs have injected uncertainty into the economy and hurt key sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing and consumer goods by driving up costs. Polls show the tariffs, which economists estimate have cost the average American household about $1,100, are viewed unfavorably by most voters, likely hurting Republican candidates in several states.

Republicans celebrated a key legislative achievement last summer, with the enactment of the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which they later sought to rebrand as the “Working Families Tax Cut.” The law’s tax provisions became a focal point for the GOP during the campaign, while Democrats slammed the included health care cuts. Before passage, North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis drew scorn from Trump for opposing the measure and soon announced his retirement, opening up a pivotal Senate seat that Democrat Roy Cooper is favored to flip.

Trump kicked the mid-decade redistricting wars into high gear when he directed Texas to redraw its congressional lines, resulting in five seats getting revamped in Republicans’ favor. Other GOP-led states followed suit, though Democrats have remained competitive in several of these redrawn districts. Meanwhile, California voters approved a Democrat-drawn map aimed at helping the party flip five Republican seats, and a court-approved map in Utah gives the party a prime pickup opportunity.

Democrats had a big night in the off-year elections, with a pair of decisive gubernatorial victories: former Rep. Abigail Spanberger flipped the Virginia governor’s mansion and Rep. Mikie Sherrill won in New Jersey. The two moderates focused their campaigns on cost-of-living issues, as did progressive Zohran Mamdani in his winning race for New York mayor, giving Democrats a blueprint for 2026.

The Trump administration began sending federal immigration agents to Minnesota in late 2025, but Operation Metro Surge picked up in January and ultimately led to the fatal shootings of two people by federal agents. That in turn intensified Democratic calls to “abolish ICE” and made immigration enforcement a defining issue in Democratic primaries across the country.

Not long after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, Trump predicted that the conflict would last a few weeks. It didn’t play out that way, and the ongoing war has become a focal point of the campaign. Higher oil costs have led to higher prices, the blame for which Democrats have pinned on Trump and Republicans in Congress. While Trump’s job approval ratings had fallen before the start of the war, they’ve dropped further since then.

Facing serious sexual misconduct allegations, California Democrat Eric Swalwell, who was running for governor, and Texas Republican Tony Gonzales resigned from the House just as their colleagues were preparing to expel them from the chamber. Swalwell dropped his gubernatorial bid and Gonzales left behind an open seat that has grown increasingly competitive.

In invalidating Louisiana’s congressional map, the Supreme Court pared back the Voting Rights Act and set off a new phase in the redistricting wars, as GOP-led Southern states sought to redraw districts with substantial Black populations. Not all attempts were successful, but Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee ended up with new maps.

A week before the Republican Senate primary runoff in Texas, Trump publicly backed scandal-plagued state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s challenge to Sen. John Cornyn. Paxton went on to win that contest, but has had a tougher general election fight against Democrat James Talarico. Two other incumbents the president targeted for defeat — Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie — also lost their May primaries to Trump-backed challengers. But Trump’s endorsement power had its limits: Several of his picks, including Iowa gubernatorial hopeful Randy Feenstra, lost primaries this summer.

June 23 was a big night for Mamdani as three House candidates he endorsed, including two fellow democratic socialists, won their primaries. Two of them ousted incumbent Democrats, Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat, and a third defeated the hand-picked successor of retiring Rep. Nydia L. Velázquez.  The New York primaries kicked off a strong summer for progressive candidates in states such as Colorado, Michigan and Minnesota.

Maine Democrat Graham Platner appeared to have weathered an array of controversies when he easily won his June primary to take on Republican Sen. Susan Collins. But about a month later, he ended his campaign following a report that he had sexually assaulted a woman he once dated, which he denied. That set off a weekslong scramble for Democrats to replace him on the ballot, culminating with a party convention at which former state Senate President Troy Jackson became Democrats’ new nominee.

The sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham shocked Washington but also touched off a scramble for South Carolina Republicans to replace him on the November ballot. Gov. Henry McMaster appointed the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat, and she then won Trump’s support to seek a full term. Boosted by the president, Darline Graham went on to secure the nomination via a primary runoff, but her general election against Democrat Annie Andrews has tightened significantly.

Republicans gathered in Dallas for a first-ever midterm convention.  The two-day event offered them a chance to hone their message, fire up voters and lavish praise upon Trump, the gathering’s brainchild. Speakers, including Trump, stoked fears about democratic socialism, but polls showed the event didn’t provide the GOP with the bounce the party was anticipating. The president followed the convention with a series of rallies in red states, where he implored Americans to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Alaska’s competitive Senate race features two candidates with the same name: Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent, and retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., listed on the ballot with no party affiliation. Former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has said she was unaware of the effort to recruit the second Sullivan, but The New York Times reported that top aides to her campaign were closely involved in the ballot-stacking plan. The Trump administration is attempting to block certification of the results if the incumbent doesn’t win, but, on Sunday, a district judge dismissed the lawsuit.

Less than 48 hours before polls were set to open on Election Day, Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens served up a November surprise Sunday, endorsing Republican Mike Rogers for Senate over Abdul El-Sayed, who had narrowly bested her in an August Democratic primary. While it was unclear how much influence her late decision could have on the race, a high-profile intraparty fight was surely not how Democrats wanted to close out the campaign. Even so, the El-Sayed campaign said Sunday was its biggest fundraising day, bringing in $2.4 million.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns home, Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after losing the presidential runoff, and Latin American diplomats back their candidates in the race for United Nations secretary-general.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief.

The highlights this week: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns home, Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after losing the presidential runoff, and Latin American diplomats back their candidates in the race for United Nations secretary-general.

On Sunday, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado announced that she had returned to the country. Tens of thousands of supporters greeted her in the capital, Caracas. In a social media post, she pledged to work “for each family to be reunited, for freedom for every political prisoner, and for freedom for Venezuela.”

Machado was most recently staying in Panama after leaving Venezuela around a year ago to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. In the last few months, the Trump administration instructed neighboring governments to block her return to Venezuela, according to multiple media outlets.

Machado is an influential opponent of acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez. The United States is working with Rodríguez to revive the oil sector in Venezuela after forcibly removing President Nicolás Maduro in January. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. plans for Venezuela eventually include free elections, but no date has been set.

Though U.S. maneuvers have prompted some investments in the country’s oil sector, working-class Venezuelans are still grappling with poor economic conditions, including annual inflation exceeding 400 percent and daily, hourslong blackouts in some parts of the country.

The Trump administration says a no-bid deal it reached in August to take a partial stake in production at 17 Venezuelan oil fields will financially benefit Venezuelans. But a copy of the agreement viewed by ProPublica showed “the potential benefits to [Venezuelan] people are largely absent from the text,” whose terms “favor U.S. interests at every turn.”

Machado has called for presidential elections by mid-2027. Her team, as well as many Venezuelan analysts, argues that companies considering investing in the country will feel more secure about its regulatory environment after a vote. Elections would also allow Venezuela’s government more legitimacy to tackle macroeconomic problems.

In recent weeks, the United States acted to ease Machado’s reentry into Venezuela by telling the Rodríguez administration that it should permit the move, Rubio told journalists on Monday. The same day, the U.S. State Department announced its most detailed plans yet for when and how elections might occur.

Nominating committees chosen as part of a U.S.-backed dialogue between the Venezuelan government and opposition figures will select new judges for the top court and a separate electoral court by around the end of this year, an unnamed State Department official told reporters in a briefing.

At that point, Rodríguez is expected to declare the presidency formally vacant, triggering a six-month deadline for elections.

In a separate press briefing, Rubio responded to a question about whether Rodríguez might try to delay that timeline. He said: “I clearly intend to see this thing well in advance of the time I leave this position,” referring to the U.S. presidential transition in January 2029.

To many observers in Venezuela, the timing of Machado’s return and the State Department’s new statements on an electoral timeline was no coincidence. “María Corina’s arrival forced the United States to define a road map” toward a vote, economist Asdrúbal Oliveros said in a Wednesday radio appearance.

The U.S. plan to move toward elections is “the only game in town,” Rubio argued in his comments to the press, saying that Washington stands ready to use tools such as sanctions as leverage on the Rodríguez administration. “We have total control of Venezuela,” Trump said on Sunday.

Friday, Oct. 30, to Wednesday, Nov. 4: The United Kingdom’s King Charles III and Queen Camilla visit Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda.

Wednesday, Nov. 4, to Thursday, Nov. 5: Spain hosts Latin American leaders at the Ibero-American Summit.

Friday, Nov. 6, to Tuesday, Nov. 17: Pope Leo XIV visits Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.

U.N. sec-gen race expands. Top diplomats from Latin American and Caribbean countries gathered at the United Nations this week to make public appeals that the next secretary-general come from the region. A group of former foreign ministers published an open letter defending the same position.

Informal U.N. tradition dictates that it’s Latin America’s turn for the role, but after weeks of candidates from Costa Rica and Guyana leading straw polls, a candidate from the United Arab Emirates entered the race last week—raising the possibility that the region could lose its chance to hold the top job.

In recent days, reports suggested that Turkey was considering nominating a former foreign minister and that the Trump administration was floating the idea of backing former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

Devex’s Colum Lynch wrote on social media last week that many in diplomatic circles thought the Emirati candidate would prevail, though China still appeared to support a candidate from Latin America or the Caribbean. Latin American countries have not announced a consensus about their own top candidate.

Supporters of former Ecuadorian presidential candidate Luisa González hold campaign banners and chant slogans demanding her release outside the Modelo Police Headquarters in Guayaquil, Ecuador, on Oct. 23.Marcos Pin/AFP via Getty Images

Opposition figure detained in Ecuador. Last week, Ecuadorian authorities arrested former presidential candidate Luisa González as she faces an investigation for violating campaign finance rules. González is now in pretrial detention; she denies wrongdoing. The arrest triggered fresh criticism that Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa is targeting political opponents.

This year, Ecuadorian authorities have blocked multiple opposition parties from competing in local elections scheduled for November. They include González’s left-wing Citizen Revolution Movement; the Amigo movement, which Citizen Revolution members hoped to use to run for office following that ban; the left-wing Unión Popular; and the centrist Construye.

In August, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights issued a public statement of concern about the mounting legal challenges for opposition actors in Ecuador, calling on the government to “ensure pluralist political participation” ahead of the November vote.

González’s detention “deepens worries about the state of Ecuadorian democracy,” the editorial board of Ecuadorian newspaper El Mercurio wrote last week.

Tacos at the top. Restaurants that receive coveted Michelin ratings often suffer from pressure to maintain them. It was no different for a Mexico City taco stand. El Califa de León was Mexico City’s first taco stand to earn the distinction in 2024. But growing pains and a dispute over who most deserved the credit led the top grillmaster to leave within months, the Washington Post reported. The taco stand lost its star this year.

The affair triggered debates in Mexico City not only about what makes a good taco stand but also why Michelin took so long to honor one after awarding street food in other parts of the world. Those curious to try the Michelin star tacos can now sample them at El Califa de León as well as at its former chef’s new restaurant, Tacos Versalles.

Which of the following taco ingredients is least historically associated with Mexican tacos?

Hard-shell tacos are more associated with the Tex-Mex taco tradition than Mexican. Cotija cheese is from Michoacán, birria-style cooked meat is from Jalisco, and salsa fresca dates to the time of the Aztecs.

Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro and his daughters arrive at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport in Miami on Oct. 28. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Enjoy our recent coverage of Brazil’s election: All FP links below are free to read.

A little over a day after Machado returned to Venezuela, another Latin American politician fled his country: Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday’s presidential election to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who also left Brazil after losing to Lula in 2022. He was later convicted of plotting a coup.

Brazil’s Supreme Court is investigating the younger Bolsonaro in multiple probes into alleged financial irregularities and money laundering. A Brazilian Supreme Court judge ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his passport on Monday after being briefed by police that he might try to run.

Though he said in a video posted that day that he would never flee Brazil, Bolsonaro and his family carried out a secret journey through Argentina and Ecuador to the United States between Tuesday and Wednesday. Trump advisor Jason Miller helped with the arrangements, the Wall Street Journal reported.

On Wednesday, Bolsonaro baffled observers with a public letter proclaiming himself the rightful president-elect of Brazil, then quickly editing it to simply call himself Brazil’s “leader.” Multiple Brazilian news organizations reported Thursday that the Trump administration communicated to Bolsonaro that it did not support him declaring himself president-elect.

The letter suggested that Bolsonaro was seeking to rally international backing for his claim of election fraud. But that support would have likely been limited: Leaders around the world—including right-wing Latin American presidents—overwhelmingly recognized Lula’s victory, and Bolsonaro’s campaign coordinator said he saw no evidence of fraud.

The United States had not yet recognized Lula’s win as of Thursday, when Trump said he did not want to comment on the election, calling it a “disgrace.” On Wednesday, he said he wouldn’t “get involved” in the controversy over Bolsonaro.

Meanwhile, one of Bolsonaro’s competitors for leadership of Brazil’s right, São Paulo Gov. Tarcísio de Freitas, posted a video on Tuesday saying the “election is over” and suggesting that Brazil move on. Though Flávio Bolsonaro’s trip to the United States may have allowed him to avoid prosecution, he may have also ceded leadership of the political field.

Catherine Osborn is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Latin America Brief. She is a print and radio journalist based in Rio de Janeiro. X: @cculbertosborn

#6062. Collins accuses Schumer of pushing attack ads filled with 'outright lies' in tight Maine race

The Republican senator defended her bipartisan record and said she is more optimistic than ever about her chances of defeating Troy Jackson.

Sen. Susan Collins on Sunday blasted Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Party over what she described as a wave of false attack ads targeting her and other Republican candidates, saying she has never seen a campaign with "so many outright lies."

She made the remarks during an interview with Fox News on Sunday, just two days before Election Day in Maine, where she is seeking re-election in a closely watched race against Democratic rival Troy Jackson. According to the latest Fox News poll, the two candidates are tied at 49%.

Collins accused Democrats of following "Chuck Schumer's playbook," pointing to attack ads she said were nearly identical to those targeting other Republican lawmakers.

MANCHIN CALLS SCHUMER 'CRAZY' FOR TRYING TO OUST GOP SENATOR IN CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, said she is more optimistic than ever despite facing a tight race and attack ads she attributed to Chuck Schumer’s political "playbook." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"One of the outrageous, completely false ads against me had to do with Jeffrey Epstein. And it turns out, in talking to two of my colleagues who are in tough races, that they had virtually identical ads run against them. So this is part of Chuck Schumer's playbook," she said.

"There are a lot of differences between my opponent and me, but I've never seen a campaign with so many outright lies. It's very frustrating," she added.

Collins further accused Democrats of trying to shift the focus away from local issues and toward divisive national political battles.

"It's certainly an attempt by my opponent and Chuck Schumer and their allies to nationalize this race," she said.

SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Susan Collins accused Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, pictured, of orchestrating a campaign of "outright lies" against Republicans as she fights to hold her Maine Senate seat. (Reuters)

Turning to her own campaign, Collins portrayed herself as a bipartisan lawmaker willing to work across party lines, arguing that the Senate needs more centrists as moderates increasingly leave Washington.

"Unfortunately, a lot of them have given up and retired or decided they just didn't want to run again. And that's one reason I am running again," she said.

"We need more people who are willing to work across party lines. That is really important," she said.

FOX NEWS POLL: NAIL-BITER IN MAINE SENATE RACE

The longtime Republican senator defended her bipartisan record and independence from Trump as she seeks another term in a closely watched race against Democratic challenger Troy Jackson. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images; Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

She also described herself as the "most independent senator on either side of the aisle," pointing to her voting record and saying her decisions are based on what she believes is right, rather than who occupies the White House or what President Donald Trump supports.

"There's this phony figure out there that I voted with President Trump 95% of the time. That's based on a sample of only 30% of the votes. If you look at a broader sample of 90% of the vote, that drops significantly to like 72%. And I voted against the president's policies 138 times," she said.

While Jackson previously told Fox News that he believes he has a "good shot" at defeating Collins, the longtime Republican senator touted strong voter support and said she is more optimistic than ever about her reelection chances.

"I'm feeling very optimistic based on the great response I get in visiting communities all over the state," she said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

#6061. What Life Is Like by the Strait of Hormuz Right Now

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Dispatch: What Life Is Like by the Strait of Hormuz Right Now

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

BANDAR ABBAS, Iran—Along Iran’s main highway south, debris lies scattered across the road, while bridges and tunnels are damaged or destroyed. Half-buried in the dirt, a broken road sign points toward Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city and the gateway to the Strait of Hormuz.

“The war has never stopped here,” said Khaleh Zeynab, 51, a food vendor working alongside Bandar Abbas’s corniche. She gestures toward the beach and the strait. “My son Reza is out there fighting. He’s been working on a ship since the beginning of the war. I know he could be killed at any moment, and that scares me, but he’s a soldier. If he doesn’t do his job, somebody else has to. We have to defend our country.”

BANDAR ABBAS, Iran—Along Iran’s main highway south, debris lies scattered across the road, while bridges and tunnels are damaged or destroyed. Half-buried in the dirt, a broken road sign points toward Bandar Abbas, Iran’s main port city and the gateway to the Strait of Hormuz.

“The war has never stopped here,” said Khaleh Zeynab, 51, a food vendor working alongside Bandar Abbas’s corniche. She gestures toward the beach and the strait. “My son Reza is out there fighting. He’s been working on a ship since the beginning of the war. I know he could be killed at any moment, and that scares me, but he’s a soldier. If he doesn’t do his job, somebody else has to. We have to defend our country.”

When the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran began on Feb. 28, residents in Bandar Abbas watched ships burn, missiles streak across the sky, and fighter jets fly overhead. Months later, explosions from the strait can still be heard almost daily, though it is not always clear whether they are air defense interceptions or fresh attacks.

What is clear, however, is that the war has made life increasingly difficult for communities whose livelihoods depend on the Strait of Hormuz.

Khaleh Zeynab sells bread in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

“It’s been tough to make ends meet,” Zeynab said. Before the war, Bandar Abbas drew tourists from across Iran as well as abroad. Since the fighting began, visitors have largely disappeared, while many residents—seeking safety after repeated attacks on the city—left for smaller villages elsewhere in Hormozgan province. At the same time, prices have surged across Iran, especially in urban centers. Food costs have risen sharply, often even doubling, adding to the pressure on families already struggling to get by.

Pouring dough onto a makeshift stove propped up on the sidewalk to make tomoshi, a thin flatbread popular in southern Iran, Zeynab said she is now helping her daughter-in-law care for her three children while Reza is away. He has returned home only once since the war began and has yet to meet his youngest daughter, born just two months ago.

“That’s what this war is doing to us,” Zeynab said with a shrug.

A road sign pointing toward Bandar Abbas, damaged in the U.S. attack on the Shur River bridge, on Sept. 19.

The war has left its mark on Bandar Abbas, too, home to roughly 700,000 people and the economic powerhouse of southern Iran. A critical gateway for imports and exports, the city handles up to 90 percent of Iran’s container shipping, and more than half of the country’s maritime trade passes through its ports.

Several ports, including the city’s fishing port, have been targeted in attacks. So has the Shur River bridge outside the city, which connects Hormozgan to neighboring Kerman province, as well as the provincial center of Iran’s state broadcaster, IRIB. The latter was “completely destroyed by 24 missiles,” said Ahmad Hosseini, a 64-year-old construction worker who witnessed the attack. “So what?” he added. “We will just rebuild it.”

Workers rebuild the Shur River bridge outside Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

The Shur River bridge, which was destroyed in a U.S. attack, on Sept. 19.

Ahmad Hosseini, a construction worker, shows us missile fragments he collected from around a damaged building, where they had been scattered by the impact, in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 20.

In recent weeks, attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz have intensified, pushing oil prices once again above $100 a barrel. U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened further strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. Tehran, meanwhile, has signaled that it is preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities and issued threats against Washington and its allies. At the same time, Iran continues to seek a diplomatic solution. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said recently that Tehran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days remained on the table—an offer that Iran submitted in mid-September, following the collapse of an interim cease-fire. Negotiations have stalled, however, with Iran’s security chief saying the United States had failed to address all seven conditions Tehran had set for reopening the waterway.

For coastal Iranians, however, the strait is more than a geopolitical chokepoint or negotiation tool; it is their lifeline. Fishermen, shipbuilders, tour guides, port workers, and smugglers all depend on the sea—which has now become the war’s front line—for their livelihoods.

Fishermen work by the roadside after a day’s catch in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 22.

Amir, 24, has spent the past five years smuggling alcohol across the strait from Oman and the United Arab Emirates. He declined to give his full name or be photographed, knowing that doing so could get him into trouble with the authorities. He grinned sheepishly as he explained how the operation worked.

Smugglers on either side of the strait use small speedboats to meet at sea, coordinating their movements over radios. Sometimes, Amir and his small crew travel deep into the strait, and on other trips, they cross all the way to the opposite shore.

It is dangerous work, even for someone who knows these waters as well as Amir does. The war has made the business even more precarious, but the income is good, he explained, especially amid soaring inflation and a battered economy.

Amir was still smuggling booze when the war broke out but was caught by the Omani coast guard and spent two months in prison in Khasab, Oman, he said. “After my release, I was deported to Afghanistan. The Taliban then sent me back to Iran,” he said, adding that he didn’t know why he was first sent to Iran’s eastern neighbor.

Twelve-year-old Mohammad works for Amir, who asked not to be photographed, selling shisha along the water in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19.

Since returning, Amir has been serving shisha at a seaside park in the city. He still regularly hears explosions from the strait, which is why he has taken a break from smuggling. But despite the risks, he wants to return.

“My father is a smuggler, too,” he said. “This is where the money is.”

For Ahmad Mokhtari, a shopkeeper in a small village just outside Bandar Abbas, the conflict has brought an unexpected opportunity to make money.

Recent war games highlight how Washington can improve its air defenses so the next round of fighting isn’t worse.

Some dramatic long-term consequences are just beginning to come into view.

But the continued shortfall of refined products means little relief at the pump.

“Many people have moved out of the city to be safer, and this has given many villages a strange boost. I used to come to the city once a month to shop. Now I’m traveling here every single day. Demand in the village has grown so much.”

Bandar Abbas, meanwhile, has yet to return to full capacity. Fishermen cannot venture as far into the strait as they used to, and some ports are operating at reduced capacity. Still, a kind of normalcy has returned.

The beach in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 19, where crowds gather for picnics after sunset as the weather cools down.

Twenty-three-year-old Kiana (foreground) poses for a portrait at the seaside on Sept. 19. She traveled to Bandar Abbas from Kerman with her family for a holiday.

In the evenings, when the heat and humidity become more bearable, people venture out along the corniche to meet friends, catch the sea breeze, grab a snack, or pose for photographs. It’s a laid-back atmosphere as the streets fill up. There’s music in the air, and occasionally, some people even dance.

But farther out, tankers remain stranded in the strait, some of them visible from the shoreline. The occasional sounds of explosions are carried across the water.

A beached boat near the shore of Bandar Abbas on Sept. 20. Locals offer conflicting accounts of its provenance; some say it was not there before the war and others that something happened to it during the conflict with the United States and Israel.

“We’ve gotten used to it,” Zeynab said. “The explosions and fighter jets are normal to us now.”

A woman wades offshore in Bandar Abbas on Sept. 23.

Stefanie Glinski is a journalist who covers conflicts and crises with a focus on the wider Middle East. X: @stephglinski

Mohammad Mohsenifar is a journalist based in Tehran.

#6059. AI Is a Choice

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

The Narrow but Feasible Path to Collective Good

Alex Imas, Mohamed A. El-Erian, and James Manyika

Few technologies in history have matched the potential of artificial intelligence to transform the economic landscape in which they emerged. Deployed broadly and effectively, AI can make workers more efficient, enable more dynamic entrepreneurship, and lift economic growth, all of which could be necessary bulwarks against the powerful economic headwinds brought on by aging populations and mounting public debt. AI can also make possible revolutionary new advances in science and medicine and democratize access to knowledge once reserved for the select few.

But the acceleration of AI also carries risks. It could be applied in ways that displace workers, disrupt how students learn, create new bioweapons and cyberweapons, and strain current supplies of energy, water, and land. Compounding these challenges is a mismatch: the benefits of this new technology may take a long time to become visible and widespread. As with earlier transformations, such as the Industrial Revolution, people are likely to experience the disruptions that come from adopting AI before they feel its benefits. And whereas users directly feel the effects of tools like chatbots, some benefits that AI is indirectly making possible, including more accurate predictions of natural disasters and improved medical diagnoses, may not be perceived as owing to the technology at all.

Public opinion has already begun to turn against AI, especially in the United States. One of the main targets has been data centers, with polls showing that a significant majority of Americans oppose the construction of data centers in their communities. Opposition to data centers needed for the new AI economy now cuts across party lines and age groups. Numerous surveys have found that residents worry about data centers using too many resources, creating endless noise, and raising their utility bills, all while developers benefit from public subsidies at the communities’ expense.

Although some of these problems are local, they also reflect wider concerns about AI. Some leading figures in AI have no doubt contributed to this anxiety with dramatic warnings of a white-collar-job apocalypse and even the possibility that AI will lead to human extinction. These are real issues that must be understood and addressed, but the growing public pushback against AI also suggests a deeper distributional challenge: individuals, communities, and businesses are being asked to help shepherd a transformative and potentially unsettling new technology at a time when many citizens see its financial gains going to a few people whom they increasingly distrust. AI is now a major issue in American politics: candidates running in competitive elections, no matter which party they belong to, appear increasingly averse to being associated with support for AI.

These anxieties are understandable. AI adoption risks repeating the mistakes of globalization, which generated large and widely spread economic benefits but led to concentrated losses of jobs, growth, and industry in particular communities. Government support in response was insufficient or arrived too late. Although the economy gained overall from free trade, the political bargain failed to give affected workers and communities a credible stake in the gains, even as individuals benefited as consumers from lower prices. The result was a backlash that contributed to the protectionism and fragmentation that continue to plague today’s politics and society.

Turning AI’s capabilities into broadly shared and enduring prosperity requires more than investing in the technology itself. The central challenge of the AI era is coordination and cooperation across groups responsible for the many complementary investments that promote the adoption of AI, including technological diffusion, worker empowerment, firm reorganization, and infrastructure construction. Because these complementary investments must be made across different institutions and at different times, progress requires market mechanisms to encourage cooperation as well as coalitions among organizations, firms, workers, communities, and governments that can turn AI’s technological gains into widespread economic and social benefits. To borrow a concept from game theory, AI is a “cooperative game” in which the largest gains arise only when many groups coordinate, and those gains persist only when every group expects to do better as part of shared coalitions than outside them.

But coalition building requires trust, and public trust—particularly regarding technology and who benefits from it—has eroded. Grand promises of scientific and medical breakthroughs will not overcome deep-seated hostility. Durable cooperation requires giving affected groups a concrete stake in the opportunities and gains that AI generates rather than merely promising future benefits. Without that stake, the individuals and groups whose support is needed to make AI flourish could block its progress. Governments could impose stifling regulations on the industry or stop issuing data center permits, firms could decline to adopt new AI-driven systems, and workers could avoid sharing the tacit knowledge needed to make the technology useful. As the economist and Nobel Prize laureate Michael Spence once observed: “You cannot solve a cooperative game uncooperatively.” The way to ensure that society benefits from AI’s enormous potential while mitigating its risks is to make cooperation the clear choice.

AI is staking a claim to being the next general-purpose technology—one that applies across a wide array of activities, improves over time, and generates complementary innovations. Electricity was an early general-purpose technology. When inventors discovered how to commercially harness electricity in the late nineteenth century, the ability to use it to power many types of machines transformed industrial production. Computing, another general-purpose technology, used electricity to process information itself, revolutionizing sectors as varied as engineering and health care.

But AI works through a more powerful input—intelligence—which makes it possible to interpret information, predict outcomes, diagnose problems, communicate with others, and make decisions. As a result, AI can raise productivity in existing sectors: a nurse can spend less time on paperwork and devote more time to patients, engineers can more quickly develop new designs, and small firms can scale up their analytics capabilities to compete with larger competitors. It can also increase efficiency so significantly that it makes possible wholly new products and services that were otherwise too costly or complicated to deliver.

AI also goes beyond existing general-purpose technologies by transforming the process of research and discovery. By inventing new ways of optimizing scientific processes, AI opens up previously unknown possibilities, similar to what microscopes and telescopes did in earlier eras. AlphaFold, a specialized AI model for which Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared half the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is a clear example. Determining a single protein’s three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence used to take months or even years; by using machine learning, AlphaFold has predicted the structures of more than 200 million proteins, fundamentally reshaping what biologists are able to investigate.

The potential of AI is thus a combination of the Industrial Revolution, whose general-purpose technologies transformed production, and the Enlightenment, which brought about inventions for making inventions—the new instruments and new paradigms that transformed the process of discovery. AI holds the promise of providing both the productivity boost and the tools to pave the way for discoveries that can address many of the problems weighing down aging, debt-ridden societies across the world.

The latest wave of AI has diffused at unprecedented speed. Google’s Gemini app and OpenAI’s ChatGPT each now reach more than one billion monthly users. Google’s AI & Economy ATLAS, a study of how people are using the company’s AI products that two of us (Imas and Manyika) worked on, analyzed 15 million interactions in more than 150 countries. It found that AI was used in tasks in 68 percent of occupations, and these occupations made up roughly 90 percent of all U.S. employment. Even automotive technicians and industrial mechanics used AI to interpret test results and diagnose electrical faults. Another study that two of us (Imas and Manyika) ran in collaboration with MIT FutureTech found that nearly half the scientists who were surveyed used some type of AI model every day, saving them time and enabling more interdisciplinary research.

But the gains of diffusion are neither guaranteed nor automatic. AI has been adopted broadly across and within sectors, but thus far its penetration remains fairly shallow. The ATLAS study found that only 21 percent of tasks in a typical occupation have been substantially affected by the technology. According to the Anthropic Economic Index, which measures how the AI model Claude is used in workplace tasks as varied as writing software, analyzing data, and managing administrative workflows, potential use far exceeds actual use. This suggests that access has spread much faster than adoption. Incorporating AI deeply enough to allow it to live up to its potential requires a bigger transformation. A firm does not change how it operates simply by buying access to an AI coding agent. It must also invest in organizational reforms and worker training and often needs to redesign its governance structure or its product lines.

The banking sector, for example, has widely adopted AI but mostly used it to perform superficial tasks. As it is currently deployed, AI gives analysts a faster way to research companies, populate spreadsheets, and identify the sources of investment returns. Deep adoption, on the other hand, requires changing workflows and job responsibilities. A bank must decide what proprietary data to feed a model, how to protect client information, and how to verify the results of the AI models it uses. Junior employees may spend less time collecting information and more time interpreting it, forming ideas, and advising clients. But many tasks that AI can automate are also forms of training. Firms will therefore need to find ways for experienced employees to help younger colleagues acquire the skills the experienced employees once developed by producing the underlying analyses themselves.

The true economic promise of AI lies in deep and transformational adoption. This requires revamping organizational processes, preparing workers to capitalize on the new technology, and applying AI in ways that enhance productivity and innovation and improve consumer welfare. Innovations that increase output and can generate new products and services have not yet appeared at a meaningful scale. But there is enormous latent demand for many new products and services, including specialized services such as individualized tutoring, health care, and legal and financial assistance, and additional demand will emerge from completely new activities that technology will make possible. By fundamentally changing how work is done and what work can be done, AI can lower the cost of providing tailored products, making new opportunities economically viable. Serving demand that previously did not make economic sense adds new value to society rather than merely redistributing a fixed economic pie.

But enlarging the economic pie does not guarantee a smooth transition for every worker. As with globalization, the new demand that AI unlocks will not necessarily arise in the same jobs, sectors, or communities in which existing work is done. This potential mismatch risks major labor market disruption and political backlash. Public anxiety is already growing, especially among younger workers seeking entry-level positions that are the most likely to be automated by AI. One study by the Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen found that the employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in occupations most exposed to AI automation was 19 percent lower than it would have been if employment had grown at the same rate as occupations less exposed to AI disruption. Yet the overall effect of AI on jobs, including entry-level positions, remains uncertain. The Economist has estimated that AI has created around one million jobs in the United States but led to about 200,000 layoffs, and the gap between the unemployment rate among 20-to-24-year-olds and the overall unemployment rate is low compared with recent decades. Most likely, as one of us (Manyika) wrote with Spence in these pages, in 2023, some jobs will be lost, some will be gained, and many more will be permanently changed.

Harnessing AI’s potential to increase prosperity without destabilizing society requires coordination. In addition to AI companies making new models, products, and tools, infrastructure developers must build the physical systems such as data centers that underpin AI. Businesses need to supply data and drive the organizational transformation to deploy models at their full potential—not just for efficiency but also to expand existing products and services or create new ones. Employers must decide how these technologies will be used, how workflows will be transformed, and how to enable workers to be more productive. Workers have to adopt the technology and invest in learning AI-relevant skills. Local communities must provide the land for data centers and consent to the technology’s expansion. And governments need to set rules, fund foundational research, and provide social insurance to support and manage transitions for those whose work or livelihoods are displaced by AI.

Each of these groups bears unique costs, captures different shares of the benefits, answers to its own constituencies, and responds to distinct incentives. This also means that unless they coordinate—whether through market mechanisms or active cooperation—these groups could slow or block AI development. Firms might underinvest in organizational change and use AI only to cut costs rather than to expand revenues, workers might resist or slow down adoption, communities might block infrastructure, and governments might restrict development. Each action might make sense in isolation, but together they lead to a suboptimal outcome for society.

This is a classic cooperative game scenario in game theory: these groups can accomplish much more when they work in concert than when they act individually and without coordination. A coalition with a common goal does not need to be a formal organization; it can be any grouping of actors who operate in ways that allow them to coordinate decisions and contribute resources to a shared project through contracts, policies, standards, investment commitments, or political bargains. Each possible coalition can generate more growth and economic value by promoting the adoption and diffusion of AI than any one actor can by operating separately.

In an ideal world, all these actors would form a single “grand coalition” to capture as much value from AI as possible. Their complementary actions and active coordination to promote AI would kick off a virtuous cycle in which wider adoption would spur advancements that would make AI more useful for society, unlock new demand and productivity growth, and encourage more people, communities, and companies to adopt the technology and support its expansion.

Such a grand coalition, however, is a benchmark rather than a blueprint. Progress is not all or nothing; smaller, more focused coalitions can still create economic and social gains that far outweigh what each actor could achieve alone. What is needed is a stable coalition—one in which no participant or group of participants can do better by leaving and doing something on their own. In the AI economy, exiting the coalition does not mean building a rival AI system. It simply means exercising a veto on increased AI use, which could take the form of imposing a local moratorium on data centers, resisting workplace adoption of AI, or blocking new regulations that encourage AI development. Because the withdrawal of any one participant would destroy more value than that participant could ever capture alone, it is critical that every essential group prefers being inside the coalition to being outside it.

A crucial question, then, is how to share the gains of working together so that cooperation remains stable over time and no coalition member wants to leave. In the case of AI, one factor that can help drive cooperation is that the technology creates conditions for what economists call a “convex game”: because the inputs to AI are complementary, each new participant makes everyone else’s contribution more valuable, causing the gains from joining the coalition to increase at an accelerating rate. Building better computing infrastructure, for instance, makes AI models and tools more capable; more capable models and tools increase the benefits for companies that want to invest in transforming their organizational processes and retraining workers, which increases productivity and spurs innovation; and wider adoption of AI in the workplace drives the need for additional computing power, which creates incentives for more infrastructure providers to build. Once a core group starts working together, the next actor that wants to join has even more to gain.

Prices, contracts, and incentives are indispensable for building a stable coalition, and market design and competition provide the architecture that enables coordination. But markets alone will not be enough. In the case of AI, the various costs and benefits will not unfold on the same timelines for all participants; some of them will benefit long before others catch up. Public institutions are necessary. Only policymakers, for instance, can create the common rules that will allow frontier labs in the coalition to coordinate on making AI safer, and only policymakers can provide enough support for workers to adapt to the AI economy. The bitter experiences that many workers and communities felt during globalization have made coalition building harder yet even more necessary.

A workable coalition does not need to bring every participant to the same negotiating table. A national bargain can establish common terms and align incentives on issues such as AI safety standards, workforce transition support, and infrastructure permitting, and smaller agreements at workplaces and in local communities can bring needed groups on board to cooperate. At both levels, the principle is the same: each group must receive a credible stake in the upside of the economic gains that the coalition creates through the overall growth of AI.

At the national level, cooperation should focus on the groups whose participation will determine whether AI technology can scale enough to generate massive economic gains. This includes the federal government, leading labs, major infrastructure builders and providers, organized labor, and large firms deploying AI. Big business matters because its use of technology and its investments in the workforce create demand that fuels the entire supply chain. Labor organizations will want to negotiate favorable terms for workforce transition, such as expanded unemployment and wage insurance, as well as for retraining; a lack of participation from organized labor will deprive the coalition of the support needed to facilitate adoption, especially in sectors such as construction in which unions have more power. For critical infrastructure, including power grids, telecommunications networks, and payment systems, the priority needs to be cybersecurity and reliability: before they integrate AI deeply into core operations, infrastructure providers need to believe that more capable models will not expose them to catastrophic risk.

The government can establish a predictable, risk-based regulatory framework to set clear standards in potentially dangerous areas such as biosecurity and to help coordinate the testing of advanced AI systems. A national framework would preempt a fragmented patchwork of idiosyncratic state-by-state bans on low-risk commercial uses of AI. Policymakers can also support AI development by funding research on foundational questions in artificial intelligence and increasing immigration and visa pathways for highly skilled workers to attract top global talent to U.S. labs. AI model and application developers, meanwhile, can participate in safety testing, and companies building out AI capacity can make available more computing power to small businesses, nonprofits, and local governments. Infrastructure providers can construct new data centers and show their support for the communities they work in by implementing ratepayer protections and paying local taxes, and large companies can invest in worker training, organizational transformation, and new business models. Finally, organized labor can supply the skilled employees needed to build the physical infrastructure underlying AI adoption, help redesign organizational workflows within companies, and lend its political weight to promoting AI nationally.

Each group benefits more than it is expected to contribute. AI model and application developers and infrastructure providers gain a predictable development path and a skilled workforce. Large firms have access to the support they need to more deeply adopt AI and improve their productivity. Workers gain new opportunities and job security during the economic transition. Washington also stands to benefit as the economy grows and the United States maintains its global technological leadership.

AI model developers and other companies in the AI ecosystem are already working together to diffuse AI more widely. Leading developers, including Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, along with partner organizations, have embedded engineers inside large organizations to identify valuable uses of AI, redesign workflows, and integrate new technology systems into production. These efforts recognize that model access is not enough: adoption requires technical assistance, organizational knowledge, and sustained engagement. A coalition can extend this capacity to smaller firms, schools, clinics, and municipalities. For AI model and application developers, supporting diffusion expands the market and provides insurance against potential political backlash. Only if the gains of AI adoption are shared with a broad swath of organizations and the general public will citizens support the expansion of the technology in society.

Frameworks for coalition building with labor groups are also emerging. Rather than working with individual firms to sign bespoke agreements, technology developers, industry associations, and policymakers are supporting worker cooperation through existing unions, apprenticeships, and retraining programs. The International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, for example, is mobilizing its members to oppose data center moratoriums while calling for better labor agreements. Google is working with the IBEW’s partner organizations to train 100,000 electrical workers and 30,000 apprentices, giving workers access to well-paid jobs and providing developers with a source of skilled labor and the political support needed to build.

At the local level, new data centers may impose concentrated costs on communities even when they create national benefits for AI users. Developers should therefore negotiate agreements that protect ratepayers and provide tangible benefits for communities through increased local revenue, better infrastructure, and more employment opportunities. Templates for how to do this are taking shape in many U.S. states. Leading AI companies and “hyperscalers,” including Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, have signed on to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, a voluntary commitment to pay the full cost of new power generation and grid upgrades in areas where they are building data centers so that household electricity bills do not rise. These companies are also funding local workforce programs and water-restoration projects and contributing property tax revenue that will allow communities to pay for new schools and roads.

The economic benefits that AI brings will increase the stability of emerging coalitions as long as they are shared. The distribution of benefits does not need to be equal, but for groups providing complementary inputs, benefits must be apportioned according to what each group contributes and also be adjusted as the technology evolves. In practice, determining each group’s contribution is not an exact science but an ongoing structured negotiation: tools such as utility tariffs, labor agreements, and enabling policies can allocate benefits in ways that reflect the role of different groups in supporting AI expansion and adoption. The share of the upside that each coalition member receives must be large enough to make participation more attractive than obstruction. Giving key players a real stake in the economic surplus that is generated is how those who might have been potential impediments to AI become participants in, and perhaps even advocates for, the expanded use of this new technology.

Where AI substitutes for existing tasks rather than complementing them, policymakers can also learn from what went wrong with globalization. Public programs to help displaced workers can be effective, but they must be accessible enough to provide support when technological disruption occurs. Targeted parts of the federal government’s Trade Adjustment Assistance program to compensate and retrain workers affected by globalization succeeded where they were put in place—research by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that eligibility for wage insurance under the program increased reemployment, shortened the amount of time out of work, and raised cumulative earnings—but it reached only a small portion of workers. Other research found that most support was provided through disability benefits that required workers to permanently exit the labor force. With AI, policymakers will need to set up expanded wage and unemployment insurance programs and support employer-led retraining programs that help workers transition into in-demand roles before displacement occurs rather than improvise after workers begin to suffer.

A coalition does not need to be built all at once. Cooperation should start in areas in which complementary benefits are clearest and participation constraints are easiest to identify, including promoting AI adoption and worker training in particular sectors such as health care or skilled trades, and encouraging support for new data centers. At the national level, safety cooperation can grow out of partnerships between coalitions and the government. Because AI’s development trajectory remains uncertain, cooperation agreements should center on investments that could pay out across multiple plausible scenarios and can be revised as the trajectory of AI becomes clearer.

International cooperation can grow in the same way. Although AI may well eventually require cooperation among adversaries and allies alike, Washington can start by forming a U.S.-led coalition built around trusted partners willing to accept common safety and security standards. The United States could, for example, set up a coalition among trusted partners that agrees on principles and frameworks in exchange for access to technology and cooperation. This coalition will naturally widen as its terms prove workable and more countries see the benefits of participating. It could eventually include China, which, given its advanced AI capabilities, is critical to addressing AI safety issues; this will require navigating complex questions of alignment and verification, however, including how to set up trusted validation bodies and mechanisms.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision provides an instructive example of international cooperation. It began in 1974 as a small forum among national regulators in 12 advanced industrialized countries and over time developed common standards for how to supervise banks around the world without empowering an imposing supranational authority, expanding its scope as those standards proved valuable. The Basel Committee was the seed for what is now the dominant international architecture that identifies and minimizes the risks of financial instability, including setting standards for how much capital banks need to hold and how to classify the riskiness of securities held on banks’ balance sheets. A future coalition for AI standards could grow through the same combination of clear entry conditions and credible commitments that have made the Basel Committee and the International Organization for Standardization, which publishes voluntary technical standards, successful.

Harnessing the potential of AI will not be easy. Critics will immediately jump to the conclusion that there are many reasons why such coalitions will not work in practice. Labs might decide that they can earn more on their own, incumbent firms might try to convert cooperation into tools to protect their market share, and governments might promise support for workers and communities and fail to deliver, as was the case with globalization.

But there is reason to be cautiously optimistic about cooperation in the age of AI. Because the technology is still relatively early in its development, it is possible to identify the groups needed to initiate cooperation, and labs, governments, communities, employers, and labor organizations have already shown interest in different parts of the bargain. Ultimately, society does not need to choose between innovation and shared prosperity. The two can be complements: cooperation will drive growth, and sharing the gains of such growth will sustain the cooperation needed to keep it going.

ALEX IMAS is Director of AGI Economics at Google DeepMind and Roger L. and Rachel M. Goetz Professor of Behavioral Science, Economics, and Applied AI at the University of Chicago’s Booth School of Business.

MOHAMED A. EL-ERIAN is Rene M. Kern Professor of Practice at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, Chief Economic Adviser at Allianz, and Chair of the Board of Directors of the Center for Global Development.

JAMES MANYIKA is Senior Vice President at Google Alphabet and its President of Research, Labs, Technology, and Society. He is a Distinguished Fellow at Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute and a Visiting Professor at the University of Oxford’s Blavatnik School of Government.

#6057. Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa so mother can attend funeral of teen killed in Bronx shooting

Vice President JD Vance evaluates President Donald Trump’s relationship and dealings with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that President Donald Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a teenage immigrant from Ghana who was shot and killed last week in the Bronx.

"The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. "Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment.

TRUMP LEAVES STAGE MID-SPEECH TO EMBRACE PARENTS OF 12-YEAR-OLD KILLED BY STRAY BULLET IN THE BRONX

President Donald Trump and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani walk out following their meeting at Gracie Mansion on Sept. 21, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

Javits Frimpong, 15, was heading to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. on Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, according to New York City Police.

He was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

No arrests have been made in connection with the shooting. The incident remains under investigation.

"All of New York City is mourning this tragedy," the mayor said.

Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to stay with his father and begin a new life in the U.S., according to U.S. Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.

TRUMP, MAMDANI SET TO MEET AGAIN ON MAYOR’S HOME TURF AFTER MONTHS OF POLITICAL WHIPLASH

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that President Donald Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a teenage immigrant from Ghana who was shot and killed in the Bronx.

"Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him," Torres said. "Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now."

Thomas Frimpong described his son as a quiet teenager. He told reporters that he learned just days before the shooting that his son was being bullied at school.

"It was the principal who told me," Thomas Frimpong said. "He said two guys are disturbing my son, so he has suspended the two guys. My son is at school. He’s innocent, so I call him. I talk with my son, he said 'Dad, I’m okay.'"

Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities, adding that the foreign ministry "will work tirelessly with U.S. authorities to ensure justice is secured."

No arrests have been made in connection with the shooting. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

He also said he welcomes Mamdani's intervention and Trump’s "timely decision" to grant a visa to the victim's mother.

"Madam Doris Adu Gyamfi’s pain as a loving mother is unimaginable and indeed everything must be done to ensure she is present to pay her respects," the foreign minister said.

The Ghanaian government "will take care of the full cost of Madam Adu Gyamfi’s travels and also stands ready to contribute towards a dignifying funeral," he added.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
