#6054. How Israel’s Coalition Wrangling Could Play Out

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Q&A: How Israel’s Coalition Wrangling Could Play Out

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

No audio? Hover over the video player, and tap the Click to Unmute button. Subtitles are also available. Closed captioning provided by Vimeo and may contain minor inconsistencies.

Register now to watch this on-demand recording.

Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.

What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.

What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: Dahlia, you’ve covered so many elections in Israel. Why was this particular election seen as so important for the country’s future?

Dahlia Scheindlin: We definitely had record turnout, which means that the vast majority of the voters saw it that way.

I don’t think I’ve ever seen two major blocs of voters as polarized. The opposition parties won a clear majority of 67 out of 120 parliamentary seats. This is getting a bit lost in international coverage. The opposition parties have a majority, and they share the sense that the country is heading for a disaster. They believe that Netanyahu was deeply committed to his alliance with his ultranationalist, extremist, religious fundamentalist political partners, and that they had sacrificed the best interests of the country for an attack on the Israeli judiciary that was unpopular among the majority from the start of 2023.

It sparked such a social backlash that it left Israel open to attack—the worst attack in Israel’s history, obviously—and then the government refused to take responsibility for it. And the issue of the government refusing to establish an independent commission of inquiry into what happened on Oct. 7, 2023, was among the most animating issues for the opposition voters.

Those who support Netanyahu see Israel as having been attacked on numerous fronts. They believe that only Netanyahu has the kind of political savvy and international clout to be able to resist pressure to end the wars that they believe are a matter of survival. When they think about Oct. 7, they think of how close Israel was to existential destruction. In their minds, Netanyahu is the prime minister who managed to marshal Israel’s closest ally, the United States, to join Israel in its war against Iran. They believe that Israel must continue on that path. They also believe Israel must never give up any control over the West Bank or Gaza, or leave its positions in Lebanon and Syria, and that these are a matter of survival.

RA: You suggested the international media is missing the headline here. But isn’t it true that Netanyahu is better placed than we expected?

DS: First of all, I’m looking at the data. Mr. Netanyahu and the parties that are loyal to him did not achieve a majority of the votes. Netanyahu’s loyalist parties won 44 percent of the vote; 56 percent wanted Netanyahu out.

The problem is that the opposition is composed of many fragmented political parties. If the opposition can’t form an alternative, then it doesn’t really matter. The biggest elephant in the room here is that the Zionist parties of the opposition—parties representing mostly Jewish citizens of Israel—have stated time and again that they do not want to build a coalition with parties representing mostly Arab or Palestinian Israeli citizens. But ultimately, it is a completely self-imposed constraint—and, frankly, it’s racist.

RA: So Israel has a parliamentary system with many parties, and we’re now going to enter a period of coalition wrangling. But it’s also interesting to me that this election had at least some element of the personality contest that comes with a presidential system. So you’ve mentioned Netanyahu; the other figure everyone was talking about was Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party.

DS: The fact that he’s a former IDF (Israel Defense Forces) chief of staff puts him in the highest level of esteem among most Jewish Israelis. There is a constituency of people who are in the center but lean right, who prioritize security issues and believe that Israel needs to be militarily strong and a Jewish state. But beyond that, they’re not extremists; they want a liberal society that separates religion from the state and ensures the separation of powers. They’re not happy with Netanyahu’s leadership, which has tried to consolidate power in the executive. And that group has supported somebody like Eisenkot time and again.

RA: Give us some insight into how the coalition wrangling works out. Now that we know a couple of the main characters, could Eisenkot cobble together some of these other opposition parties, plus the Arab parties, and maybe try to form a government, or is Netanyahu the one who has the best shot at trying to do so? How does this all work?

DS: The various scenarios for how to reach a government are manifold, and they are all uncertain. One scenario is that nobody can build a government, and Israel goes into another election, which is the precedent we had from 2019 through 2022, when we held five election cycles for this very reason.

Another scenario is that there is a minority government, which is legal as long as it’s sworn in with more votes than those against it. It is inherently unstable, because there is a majority of parliamentary seats who could vote to disband the Knesset and call new elections. There is also a possibility—and not an unlikely one—that, for example, Netanyahu is asked to form the government by the president, and somebody from the Zionist opposition parties defects to his side.

Most Israeli parties are amalgamated factions of smaller parties. There’s a lot of speculation about a unity government between Likud and the mainstream Zionist parties, with bargaining over who would be prime minister when. That is very complex, legally and politically. Netanyahu would want to be first in any rotation; the opposition parties would not want to accept that. If he goes second in a rotation, he’s in trouble because he is legally not supposed to be serving as a regular minister since he is under indictment for three counts of corruption and has been standing trial for the last six years. But you can see how many options are on the table. None of them are great ones.

Main opposition parties fail to muster majority.

Early results indicate deadlock in parliamentary elections.

RA: It does seem like Israel is generally becoming more right-wing, more focused on its security at the cost of soft power. Netanyahu has frequently said he’s happy to turn Israel into Sparta. And it seems like what is so striking from everything you’ve said so far is that Netanyahu won a fair number of seats, and despite the opposition’s performance, he is still somewhat popular. Clearly, the differences between him and the potential opposition are not that great on some key issues on security. So what does this mean for Israel’s overall trajectory, no matter who actually forms a government after this?

DS: It’s a good observation about hard power versus soft power. Israel is a militarist society and has placed so much emphasis on the image of the omnipotent army, but of course, it was no less invested in its global image over the decades and prided itself on being part of the family of democratic nations in the West.

But in recent years, the country has unapologetically moved away from its liberal trajectory. Across the board, Israelis increasingly think that the entire world is against them, that the whole world is inherently anti-Israel and antisemitic no matter what Israel does. That goes beyond the right wing. The backlash against Israel in the immediate days after Oct. 7 was proof of concept to those who already felt that way and also really scared a lot of Israelis who didn’t necessarily think that way.

RA: But Dahlia, since you speak to so many voters and have your pulse on how Israelis think, can you play out that school of thought of feeling like everyone’s against you, of feeling that much of the region and the world is antisemitic? Where does that lead? What is the logical conclusion of that feeling?

DS: Netanyahu told us where that will lead just a day or two before the election. He said that in light of the possibility that Israel will be facing more sweeping sanctions—even more than it already is—it would have to build a separate economy that is free of the global system, and that Israel can just do that based on cryptocurrency. Nobody took it very well. But again, he maximized his vote. Netanyahu’s supporters are not deterred; they think that Israel has always been a resilient country, so they’re not as worried, whereas the Israelis who didn’t vote for the government are terrified at the idea of being shut out of the world that they want to be part of. They see themselves with a more globalist orientation.

RA: How much do regular Israelis reckon with the change in attitude toward Israel in the United States, as more and more Americans seem to be openly discussing a changing U.S.-Israeli relationship, in part because of Israel’s politics over the last few years, and in particular over Gaza and U.S. military support for Israel in that war. It doesn’t seem like this has been a change election on that front.

DS: The majority of Israelis believed it was a change election, just not in the ways the international community was looking for. I’ve never seen a bigger gap between how outsiders view Israel and how Israelis are talking about their country since Oct. 7. It’s natural that from the outside, people don’t always see the inside of any country, but I do think the gap has gotten so much bigger.

For Israelis, American attitudes are a background issue. It occasionally makes a headline when a new Pew or Gallup survey comes out showing the erosion of Israel’s position. But again, that’s when the majority of Israeli Jews return to the idea that people were probably always against Israel, and that certainly in America, they have that “woke disease” that has poisoned the public mind toward Israel and has nothing to do with Israel’s policies—even those who are critical of Israel’s policy at home. When they hear that kind of criticism from abroad, they get defensive.

People who are already opposed to the government will say that this is another thing they think is problematic or that they’re worried about. But it’s not the number one most urgent issue for them. There is an awareness of the possibility of a change in America following the midterms and an awareness of where the Democratic Party is going. But I think the presidential election and the possibility of a change of administration is too abstract for Israelis right now.

It was always a profound and frankly incomprehensible mistake to think that you could just hold people under a hostile and violent military occupation. The day-to-day reality of Palestinians is so bad that there would always be some sort of escalation. I know of no national movement seeking self-determination that has ever given up on their self-determination, no matter how good their quality of life. Palestinians have neither.

That’s the delusion in every unresolved ethno-nationalist territorial conflict, especially when the gap is so huge and one side enjoys full sovereignty—complete international integration and great economic indicators—while the other side has none of those things, nor national self-determination. There’s no reality in which that would ever go away or fail to escalate. The longer it goes on, the more extreme the escalations become.

So it’s not just bad for Israel’s foreign relations or image. Primarily, it’s bad for the Palestinians who continue living under this hostile and very violent regime, and of course for Gaza, the vast destruction of which is incomprehensible at this point. But it’s bad for Israel, too. Israel’s democracy cannot really ever be fulfilled. These are the same state institutions who are ultimately implicated in that regime, and this is what ultimately fed into the chaos that we saw in 2023.

It is also the source of the deepest divisions within Israel over the very nature of its regime, which is what was at stake in 2023 and what so many Israelis thought was at stake in this election, even if they didn’t make the connection that it’s fundamentally connected with occupation and Palestinians.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#6053. How to watch critical 2026 midterm election races in TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME and FL

FOX Business' Grady Trimble and Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya join 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss tight Senate races in Iowa and Minnesota.

Control of Congress is on the line Tuesday as voters decide pivotal Senate and House races across the country, while closely watched contests for governor will shape the political landscape in key states during President Donald Trump's second term.

Republicans are fighting to defend their congressional majorities as Democrats seek gains in battlegrounds from Texas and Georgia to Michigan and Maine. Open seats, vulnerable incumbents and competitive statewide races have put nine states at the center of the fight for power in Washington and state capitals.

With races stretching across multiple time zones, here are the key contests to watch, when polls close and how to follow live results as Election Night unfolds.

Fox News Power Rankings on midterm seat losses under President Donald Trump's economy. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Texas voters face two major statewide showdowns, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico for the Senate seat held by outgoing Republican John Cornyn, while GOP Gov. Greg Abbott seeks a historic fourth term against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK

The Senate contest has emerged as an unusually competitive race in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, pitting Paxton's conservative appeal and history of legal controversies against Talarico's campaign focused on political change.

Meanwhile, Abbott's reelection bid offers another test of Republican dominance, with border security, education and the economy shaping the fight over the state's future.

SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY

Ohio features a Senate rematch of sorts, with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown seeking a return to Washington against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's former seat. Brown is attempting a political comeback in a state that has shifted toward Republicans, while Husted seeks his first electoral victory for the Senate.

Husted's campaign also enlisted Ohio native and former NFL coach Jon "Chucky" Gruden for campaign appearances.

Voters will decide who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy facing Democrat Amy Acton. Ramaswamy's campaign recently pulled a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother after criticism from fellow Republicans, including DeWine.

Michigan's open Senate seat could prove pivotal to the balance of power in Washington, with former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers facing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the contest to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW

The Senate race has grown increasingly contentious as Rogers and Republican allies have raised allegations about El-Sayed's family's purported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, citing old social media posts by his half-sister. El-Sayed has denied any connection to the organization and publicly disavowed it, while independent fact-checkers have found no evidence establishing his personal affiliation.

The state also features a gubernatorial showdown between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Rep. John James, testing whether Michigan voters will maintain Democratic control of the governor's office or turn to Republicans.

Wisconsin's open governor's race pits Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany against Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley as voters choose a successor to Democratic Gov. Tony Evers.

The contest centers on the state's political direction, including taxes, public spending and education, after Crowley defeated progressive state Rep. Francesca Hong in a crowded Democratic primary.

Georgia offers two major statewide contests, with Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defending his seat against Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a state Trump narrowly carried in 2024.

Georgia Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA) speaks alongside U.S. President Donald Trump during a midterm campaign rally at the Guardian Centers on October 24, 2026, in Perry, Georgia. Trump is speaking at a rally in support of Georgia Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), who is trying to unseat the incumbent U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA), and Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson. (Alex Wong / Getty Images)

Ossoff's race will test whether Democrats can hold a Senate seat in a state that has delivered closely contested presidential and Senate elections, while the open governor's race between Republican businessman Rick Jackson and former Democratic Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will determine who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp.

Iowa voters will decide whether Republicans can retain two major offices in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the Senate seat being vacated by Republican Joni Ernst, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand faces Republican Zach Lahn in the open governor's race to succeed retiring longtime GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds.

Although the Hawkeye State has shifted toward Republicans in recent election cycles, Democrats previously enjoyed sustained statewide success through figures including former Sen. Tom Harkin and former Gov. Tom Vilsack.

The contests will test whether Democrats can regain ground, with affordability, agriculture and state economic policy among the central issues.

Nevada's marquee contest features Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo seeking another term against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford.

The race will test whether Republicans can retain the governor's office in a state where Democrats have remained competitive in statewide elections, with housing affordability, education and public safety among the issues facing voters.

Lombardo, the former Clark County sheriff, defeated incumbent Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022, with Ford now hoping to hit the jackpot in Carson City.

Maine's Senate race pits longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins against former Democratic state Senate President Troy Jackson in one of the country's most closely watched contests.

Collins is seeking another term in a blue-leaning state that supported Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Meanwhile, Jackson is attempting to turn Maine's Democratic presidential voting pattern into a Senate pickup after replacing Graham Platner, who withdrew as the Democratic nominee following a sexual assault allegation that he denied.

Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, faces off against Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president and the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, in their fourth debate appearance together on Thursday evening. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images; Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

The contest will test Collins' longstanding crossover appeal and could have major consequences for the Senate's balance of power, as she remains New England's only Republican member of Congress.

Florida voters will choose a successor to term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, with Republican Rep. Byron Donalds facing former Republican congressman-turned-Democrat David Jolly.

The race presents a contest over the future of Florida's government, including affordability, immigration and the direction of state policy.

Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, appointed to the seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, also faces DSA-affiliated Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special Senate election, while competitive House contests could affect the national congressional picture.

As polls close across the country's biggest battlegrounds on Tuesday, Nov. 3, Fox News Channel and Fox News Digital will deliver live results, race calls and analysis of the contests that could determine control of Congress.

Viewers can watch live coverage on Fox News Go with a participating television provider or stream Fox News Channel through FOX One.

Fox News Channel's special "FOX News Democracy 26" coverage begins at 6 p.m. ET Tuesday, co-anchored by Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum.

Dana Perino, Brit Hume, Harold Ford Jr., Bill Hemmer, Sandra Smith, Laura Ingraham, Jesse Watters, Sean Hannity and other Fox News personalities will contribute throughout the evening.

The Fox News Decision Desk will provide race calls for House, Senate and gubernatorial contests, along with projections of which party will control each chamber of Congress.

FOX Business will simulcast Fox News Channel's Election Night coverage from 6 p.m. Tuesday until 6 a.m. Wednesday. Trace Gallagher will lead overnight coverage, with a special early edition of "FOX & Friends First" beginning at 4 a.m.

On Fox News Digital, readers can follow a live Election Night blog featuring breaking developments, Fox News Power Rankings and Fox News Voter Analysis as polls close across the country.

The Fox News Elections Center will serve as a central destination for tracking results in Texas, Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin, Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Maine and Florida, as well as other key congressional and statewide races nationwide.

The Fox News app will feature a new "Midterms 2026" tab with interactive county-level election maps and an AI-powered "Election HQ" chatbot that answers questions about races and results using Fox News reporting.

Signed-in users can also participate in "The Room," an interactive Election Night discussion experience featuring real-time commentary.

For additional election analysis, "Ruthless Live! Midterm Election Show" will stream from 8 to 11 p.m. ET on Fox News Digital and FOX Nation.

Listeners can tune in to Fox News Radio or use the Fox News app's "Listen" feature beginning at 7 p.m. ET, when Jared Halpern and Jessica Rosenthal kick off live radio coverage.

More than 20 Fox News Channel and FOX Business correspondents will report from battleground states nationwide, while chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram will provide updates from Capitol Hill.

With control of the House and Senate at stake, Fox News Channel and Fox News Digital will provide continuing coverage as results emerge from the nine battleground states and beyond, including races that may remain undecided into Wednesday.

Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

#6051. The China Price

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

Beijing’s Green Path to Ending Dollar Dominance

In 1971, as the international monetary system was on the brink of collapse, U.S. Treasury Secretary John Connally told a group of worried European finance ministers that the dollar was “our currency, but your problem.” The dollar had become that system’s official reserve currency in 1944, under the Bretton Woods agreement, making signatories subject to the whims of U.S. monetary policy. Even after Bretton Woods collapsed and many currencies floated freely, the dollar continued to dominate. In the last half century, U.S. currency power has only expanded, as more countries have integrated into the global economy and therefore grown to depend on the dollar. China, reliant on export-driven growth, is foremost among them.

Reckoning with the possibility that Washington could someday make the dollar China’s problem, Beijing is now crafting its own solution. In a January 2024 speech, Chinese leader Xi Jinping made this effort explicit, instructing senior provincial and ministerial officials to accelerate China’s transformation into a “leading financial power.” A strong currency, he specified, was one of the essential foundations of that power. When Qiushi, the Chinese Communist Party’s flagship journal, published the full text of the speech in 2026, the standard Xi had in mind became clearer: for a currency to be considered “strong,” it must be widely used in international trade, investment, and foreign exchange markets and be recognized as a global reserve currency.

Xi’s call is the latest episode in a long history of efforts by major powers to reduce their dependence on the dollar-centered global financial system. In 1965, French Finance Minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing famously described the disproportionate advantages that dollar dominance confers on the United States as “exorbitant privilege”; the same year, France began aggressively converting a substantial share of its dollar reserves into gold, contributing to the collapse of the Bretton Woods system. In 1999, the Japanese government released a report on how to promote wider international use of the yen. That same year, the launch of the euro gave Europe what would become the world’s second most important international currency, affording it greater monetary autonomy even as the European Central Bank carefully danced around any suggestion that it might challenge the dollar.

What distinguishes Xi’s ambition is that China, unlike Europe or Japan, possesses the economic heft, military capability, and political will to rival the United States’ geopolitical power. Not since London commanded a global empire has another country’s currency stood a realistic chance of competing with the dollar. A global financial transition from “In God We Trust” to “Where the Party Leads, We Follow” can no longer be dismissed as fantasy.

The internationalization of the renminbi would afford China a measure of financial survivability should the United States ever choose to wield the dollar as a punitive weapon, as it did against Russia after the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The United States controls both the supply of the dominant global reserve currency and many of the critical financial infrastructure chokepoints through which it circulates. Washington, if it so desired, could severely restrict China’s access to dollar liquidity by making the cost of doing business with Chinese institutions prohibitive, for example by indicting or sanctioning a major Chinese bank. Any such measure would shock the Chinese financial system, raise transaction costs for trade, and deliver a major competitive blow to China’s export sector, which accounts for roughly one-fifth of its GDP.

Survivability, however, is only a prerequisite for credible deterrence. To deter the United States from using the dollar weapon, Beijing requires a financial second-strike capability. It must be able to redirect a substantial share of global trade and finance to a renminbi-based network. The durability of that shift depends on healthy global demand for an anchor asset priced in renminbi. For China, the most likely source of such an anchor asset lies in its dominance of the green economy.

Xi does not necessarily want the renminbi to replace the dollar. His 2024 speech advocated strength, not hegemony. Placing a respectable second, or even a consequential third, would suffice to break the dollar’s effective monopoly and constrain the United States’ ability to impose financial sanctions unilaterally, while saving China the effort and cost of sustaining currency supremacy. From Beijing’s perspective, the mission is to establish the renminbi as the Pepsi to the dollar’s Coca-Cola: never the market leader, but serviceable in a pinch and more than capable of keeping the dominant incumbent honest.

The near-universal acceptance of the U.S. dollar arguably benefits China more than any other country. The Chinese economy relies on exports, and Chinese goods priced and financed in dollars can reach ready buyers almost anywhere. The resulting profits can then be invested almost anywhere and converted into liquid funds on short notice. This suits Beijing: China enjoys the benefits of global liquidity without bearing the burdens of sustaining it. To preserve the global dollar system, the United States must tolerate foreign ownership of an ever-expanding volume of dollar claims as countries conduct ever more business in the currency. U.S. markets are exposed to international volatility, and foreigners hold some influence over U.S. corporations. The Federal Reserve, which issues the dollar, backstops the system, expanding its balance sheet during periods of financial stress, when governments and private companies hoard dollars to ensure they can continue to pay their debts and buy goods. This openness and exposure has posed little threat to the U.S. economy because foreign shareholders have generally sought to operate within, rather than change, U.S. business norms, and U.S. banks have earned tidy profits intermediating the world’s capital flows through New York and London.

China’s leaders have no desire to make any such tradeoff. Maintaining a global renminbi system would be fundamentally at odds with China’s state-led economic model. For the renminbi to replicate the dollar’s functions, China would have to create broad, two-way financial channels through which foreign holders of renminbi could reinvest that money into the Chinese economy. The resulting capital inflows would fundamentally reshape China’s domestic financial markets. It would be impractical for Beijing to confine foreign investors to a narrow group of approved assets, as it does now. Once foreign investors were allowed into China’s markets in force, they would arbitrage the distortions created by financial repression and politically directed capital allocation. Such competition would undermine one of Beijing’s most effective means of securing the loyalty of China’s business class: controlling who gains access to capital, on what terms, and for what purposes.

For many wealthy Chinese citizens, including some members of the Communist Party itself, the dollar is an indispensable form of political risk insurance. Domestic political rivalries can lead to asset seizure or even imprisonment with little due process. Offshore dollar deposits and foreign corporate structures allow elites to diversify their holdings across currencies and jurisdictions. Control of a company listed overseas, especially in the United States, offers wealthy Chinese more than prestige and access to global capital; disclosure obligations, duties to shareholders, and international visibility, which extend beyond the party’s control, can give Chinese executives leverage against arbitrary demands from officials at home. These constraints cannot prevent interference by senior authorities determined to pursue their targets, but they can raise its cost, slow its implementation, and create room for negotiation. The dollar-based system is a refuge for Chinese elites who fall from grace, and because no one’s position is ever entirely secure, few wish to see that refuge disappear.

China is perfectly willing to go on living in a world that the dollar makes go round. But it cannot abide the dollar’s weaponization, and the renminbi still has a long way to go before it is strong enough to blunt that threat. If more countries and businesses are to adopt the renminbi, there must first be a global financial infrastructure for its use. China has already laid the foundation by facilitating renminbi use among firms in more than a hundred countries and across a growing array of commodity markets to settle transactions, obtain financing for trade and investment, and hedge their risks. Here, breadth matters far more than depth. Even modest daily volumes of renminbi transactions can keep payment channels operational, preserve financial relationships, and maintain the legal and administrative expertise needed to run an alternative financial system.

Because China’s relative economic strength lies in the flow of manufactured goods—it accounted for 20 percent of global manufactured exports in 2025—Beijing has concentrated its efforts on building a payment network that facilitates the commercial flows generated by its manufacturing machine. In 2005, Zhou Xiaochuan, then governor of the People’s Bank of China, publicly encouraged the already increasing use of local currencies among China’s trading partners. In 2009, the PBOC launched a pilot program for settling cross-border transactions in renminbi, followed in 2015 by the creation of the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System, the backbone of China’s international renminbi network. CIPS began with 195 participants spanning 50 countries; by June 2026, it had 1,829 participants and could route payments to more than 5,200 banking institutions in 191 countries. But CIPS remains much smaller than the mature wholesale payment systems supporting the dollar and the euro. In 2025, the U.S.-based Clearing House Interbank Payments System processed an estimated 19 times as much value in international payments as CIPS, and Europe’s real-time gross settlement system, called T2, cleared about 14 times as much.

But payments alone are a misleading measure of currency power. An international transaction entails far more than a transfer of economic value; it requires a package of financial services that unfolds across five linked stages: pricing, financing, risk transfer, payment, and reinvestment. The dollar dominates international trade and finance because it is the default currency at every stage, with its strength in each reinforcing its position in all the others. For the renminbi to supplant the dollar, it would have to become competitive at every stage of the transaction cycle, not just in payments.

China’s leaders recognize that the influence of financial centers in London, New York, and Tokyo rests not only on their ability to move money but also on their institutions’ ability to create credit, set prices, insure shipments, and recycle savings. That is why Chinese state-owned enterprises are driving the expansion of the renminbi network. By denominating invoices, contracts, and overseas project financing in renminbi, these enterprises create a base of recurring demand for the currency around which Chinese banks, insurers, and other financial institutions can build competing business lines under Chinese control. To reinforce that base, the Communist Party laid out an action plan in 2025 that instructs state-owned enterprises to prioritize settlement in renminbi, rather than dollars, whenever they deal with foreign suppliers and customers. That strategy is already fostering a regional network for renminbi use in Southeast Asia. In 2024, renminbi payments involving economies in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations rose 19 percent, with two-thirds of those transactions occurring between ASEAN countries.

Beijing has largely completed the first phase of its strategy, establishing a foothold in payments, and it is now expanding upstream into pricing, financing, and risk transfer, and, cautiously, downstream into reinvestment. Only recently has Beijing begun to appreciate how much the currency in which goods are priced influences the subsequent stages of the transaction cycle. Historically, China has been content to price the goods it imports and exports mostly in dollars. According to International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates, only 6.5 percent of China’s exports were invoiced in renminbi in 2023. Chinese government statistics show that nearly 30 percent of China’s trade in goods is settled in renminbi, but much of that is essentially a dollar transaction masquerading as a renminbi one: Chinese exporters invoice in dollars, buyers obtain dollar funding and are debited in dollars, and the funds are converted into renminbi only just before reaching the mainland.

The government is seeking to reverse that pattern by promoting what it calls “China prices”: renminbi-denominated benchmark prices listed on local exchanges for major commodities that China imports. Greater autonomy over pricing means that Chinese firms can buy raw inputs and manage their exposure to commodity price swings in global markets without acquiring dollars. It also gives Chinese authorities greater influence over the reference prices used to set the terms of supply contracts for the physical delivery of those commodities. This leverage is vital for China because the steady flow of raw inputs is essential to the smooth running of its manufacturing machine.

Price autonomy matters especially for critical minerals, which feed the green industries that in Xi’s view are central to China’s economic future. China produces more than 80 percent of the world’s batteries and consumes over 75 percent of its lithium, 70 percent of its cobalt, and about 60 percent of its nickel. But the country’s position in global markets for each of these minerals does not yet reflect its dominance in production and consumption. To date, China has made the most progress in lithium; more than 90 percent of global trading in lithium-carbonate futures occurs on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange, where contracts are denominated in renminbi. In July, the exchange allowed foreign traders to trade the lithium-carbonate futures contract directly, announcing with fanfare that several overseas “leading enterprises” had joined the market. China is now poised, perhaps for the first time in modern history, to become the principal financial center for a globally important commodity. Nickel and cobalt, on the other hand, remain tied to dollar benchmarks in London and Chicago. Although China is the largest consumer of these two minerals, it is not yet the financial reference point for their markets. That is the sort of mismatch that the push for China prices is meant to resolve.

The financing stage of Beijing’s renminbi strategy is gaining momentum. In 2023, Beijing instructed Chinese financial institutions to expand their renminbi funding abroad. State-backed lenders such as the Export-Import Bank of China have increased their renminbi lending for overseas trade and infrastructure projects, and commercial banks increasingly supply renminbi trade finance. Between 2023 and mid-2026, Chinese financial institutions more than doubled their renminbi lending to overseas borrowers from 1.3 to 2.9 trillion yuan ($428 billion). The PBOC, for its part, has adopted currency swap agreements with 32 foreign central banks and monetary authorities, including those in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as the European Central Bank. In their early years, after the global financial crisis, these swap lines were largely symbolic and only lightly used, but in recent years, some have provided direct support for commercial activity. In 2025, Turkish companies borrowed four billion yuan ($557 million) to pay Chinese suppliers using a facility backed by a PBOC swap line, 70 percent more than they had borrowed a year earlier. This effort to turn the renminbi into a funding currency is starting to gain traction: in May 2026, the renminbi accounted for seven percent of the value of trade-finance messages on SWIFT, the leading global platform for exchanging payment instructions, up from 5.1 percent two years earlier and enough to overtake the euro for second place, although the dollar remained leagues ahead with an 82.5 percent share.

Beijing has also taken steps, if more modest ones, to increase the renminbi’s presence in markets for insurance and reinsurance. In 2025, Bank of China, a state-owned bank, and PICC, a state-owned property and casualty insurance company, developed new terms under which premiums and claims for cargo shipments could be settled in renminbi. The terms also specified Shanghai as the preferred venue for arbitration, part of a broader effort to shift the maritime-insurance market away from its traditional reliance on dollar settlement and English commercial law, long the standard framework for international shipping and maritime insurance contracts.

The final stage of the transaction cycle, reinvestment, completes the loop through which goods and value circulate through the global economy. Recipients of payment must decide what to do with the proceeds: hold them in a short-term account, invest them in longer-term assets, or convert them into another currency. A strong currency ecosystem becomes sustainable at scale only when recipients are willing to hold and reinvest their balances rather than routinely convert them.

Beijing has, over the past decade, given foreign holders of renminbi more ways to reinvest their balances. The Stock Connect and Bond Connect programs, which took their earliest forms in 2014 and 2017, respectively, have since expanded to allow a much broader mix of investors outside China to use renminbi to buy some mainland equities and bonds. Before these programs began, licensing and quotas restricted direct access to Chinese markets, with only about 228 large institutional investors receiving quotas in 2013; today, about 1,000 investors have that status. In 2025, foreign trading through Stock Connect averaged 212 billion yuan ($29.5 billion) per day, and Bond Connect averaged 39 billion yuan ($5.4 billion) per day. The tools available to manage the risks associated with these investments have also expanded. Swap Connect, launched in 2023, allows offshore investors to hedge against movements in onshore renminbi interest rates.

Access to China’s financial markets is no longer the biggest problem facing foreign investors, but the risk that Beijing’s unpredictable capital controls could someday trap their funds remains a worry. A 2023 survey by the Insurance Asset Management Association of China and J.P. Morgan Asset Management found that roughly two-thirds of chief investment officers at insurance companies outside China cited controls on capital moving in and out of the country as a top concern for investing there. Despite greater access than ever, foreign investors remain reluctant to hold Chinese assets at scale. In March 2026, they held only 3.2 trillion yuan ($448 billion), or 1.6 percent of the Chinese bond market, compared with roughly $15.5 trillion, or 27 percent, of the U.S. bond market. Reserve holdings recorded with the IMF reveal an even wider gap: in the first quarter of 2026, the renminbi accounted for just under two percent of global foreign-exchange reserves, compared with 57 percent for the dollar. Without a far larger pool of renminbi assets that foreigners can freely buy and sell, the renminbi cannot come close to replacing the dollar.

For China to wield anything approaching the currency power of the United States, the renminbi must dominate trade in a good that China controls and the rest of the world cannot easily do without. In the dollar system, the global oil trade has long played this role—hence the term “petrodollar.” In a renminbi-ascendant system, the corresponding anchor could be the critical minerals, clean energy equipment, and electrical infrastructure that are central to green energy technology. If China consolidates its dominance over that industrial ecosystem, using its scale and cost advantages to prevent competitors from catching up, it could gain enough leverage to price those essential, hard-to-substitute exports in renminbi, creating the foundation for a “green yuan” that might eventually replace the petrodollar.

China has spent decades methodically assembling the supply chains that have made it the world’s dominant producer of green energy technology and equipment. Beijing is now on the verge of taking a commanding position across a set of goods that the world has decided it cannot do without. China’s strategy rests on vertical integration of nearly the entire clean energy supply chain. It is the leading refiner of 19 of the 20 energy-related strategic minerals tracked by the International Energy Agency, with an average market share of 70 percent. It accounts for roughly 85 percent of global solar panel manufacturing capacity, and it supplies 78 percent of the wind-turbine capacity installed worldwide. In 2025, it produced about 70 percent of the world’s electric vehicles.

After decisively seizing the first-mover advantage, Beijing is now consolidating its market position, using economies of scale to undercut prospective rivals and promote technical standards built around technologies owned by Chinese firms. The green energy economy is more diffuse than the fossil fuel system it seeks to replace and therefore more difficult to command. But China is already beginning to turn its market-share lead into structural advantages that could lock out competitors and entrench its dominance.

Until recently, Beijing focused more on extending its industrial lead in green energy than on converting that advantage into financial power. But that is beginning to change. The proliferation of carbon-neutral investment mandates has unintentionally created a green finance industry almost tailor-made for China. In 2022, Beijing published its “Green Bond Principles,” which require green bond issuers to allocate 100 percent of proceeds to eligible green projects.

By the end of 2025, funds dedicated to sustainable investment were worth $4.13 trillion worldwide, and assets managed according to sustainability criteria were projected to reach $40 trillion by 2030. Chinese entities, meanwhile, already had 47.2 trillion yuan ($6.7 trillion) in green loans and bonds outstanding, far exceeding any other country’s green lending, but largely confined to its domestic renminbi system. In 2024, foreign institutions held only 3.2 billion yuan ($445 million) of China’s 2.2 trillion yuan ($306 billion) green bond market, a minuscule 0.15 percent.

That meager foreign participation is likely to increase. Chinese authorities are working to turn more of the country’s vast pool of green debt—a term for loans and bonds issued for projects with a positive environmental impact—developed primarily for a domestic investor base, into tradable securities that foreign investors can hold in compliance with international sustainability mandates. Their objective is to create a broad class of renminbi-denominated assets that are internationally investable, tied to green projects, and integrated into the broader renminbi ecosystem for pricing, settlement, and other financial services.

About 17 percent of China’s green bond market has already been screened against technical criteria aligned with European green finance frameworks, making those bonds easier for foreign investors and index providers to recognize and include in their portfolios. The Ministry of Finance has begun issuing renminbi-denominated sovereign green bonds outside China, with its first bond issuance raising six billion yuan ($834 million) in London in April 2025, followed by a second six-billion-yuan issuance in Hong Kong this past May, where orders were ten times the amount on offer. These issues are tiny compared with China’s domestic market, but they establish pricing reference points that make it easier for other entities to issue renminbi-denominated green debt in the future. Pakistan’s issuance, in May, of a 1.75 billion yuan ($258 million) green Panda bond—the term for renminbi-denominated debt issued in China by foreign borrowers—offers a glimpse of a future in which foreign borrowers routinely raise renminbi in China to finance their green development.

This is how industrial dominance begins to grow into financial power. The Chinese government has no formal plans to create a green yuan, but the constituent pieces of such a system are nevertheless starting to come together. The anchor asset for a green yuan would not be green technology itself, but an expanding family of renminbi claims on the green economy. Green bonds would form this economy’s tradable core, connecting China’s industrial advantage to the growing global demand for sustainable assets.

Much of the world has set deadlines for replacing fossil fuels that cannot be met without China’s green economy. Even if the political will to combat climate change fades, global dependence on imported energy has created geopolitical vulnerabilities that will likely continue to buoy demand for renewables, which almost any country can deploy to produce more energy at home. For countries and firms seeking entry into the green economy, accepting renminbi financing and Chinese technical standards may eventually become part of the ordinary price of admission. The result would be a self-reinforcing circuit of green goods and green finance, much of it denominated in renminbi.

For Washington, the prospect of a green yuan should not set off alarms about an imminent renminbi takeover. It should instead prompt a harder question: whether the petrodollar is no longer fit for purpose and what asset class, technology, or industrial system might anchor the dollar’s currency power in the future. The dollar rests on far more than the United States’ ability to secure global energy flows and its ties with major oil-producing states, but policymakers would be mistaken to treat its supremacy as permanent.

Beijing is not plotting to dethrone the dollar, and the Communist Party almost certainly does not want the financial openness such a victory would require. Whether or not the green yuan becomes a reality someday, the more immediate value to the party of an internationalized renminbi is its potential to deter China hawks in Washington from weaponizing China’s current reliance on the dollar.

As China’s renminbi-based system becomes stronger, so will Beijing’s ability to withstand the shock of potential U.S. financial sanctions. Washington’s threat to impose those sanctions will, in turn, lose some of its potency. That shift in the economic power dynamic would likely make Beijing more willing to call Washington’s bluff—which it may already be doing. In May, China issued its first-ever blocking order, instructing firms in China not to comply with U.S. sanctions on five Chinese oil refiners alleged to be major purchasers of Iranian oil.

If the reign of King Dollar ever ends, it probably won’t be because China usurped the throne but rather because the United States surrendered it. Washington must take note that the strategic asset underpinning the next monetary order may not be a barrel of oil but an industrial ecosystem. The danger is that financial markets may provide little warning that such a transition is underway. Markets can go long stretches ignoring the mounting evidence of change before a catalyst—such as a political stalemate over raising the U.S. debt limit—finally causes models to adjust and prices to snap up or down. U.S. officials are reluctant to plan for the erosion of the dollar’s dominance for fear that doing so would signal to markets that such a decline is inevitable. Their eagerness to point to price charts as proof of the dollar’s resilience, however, suggests that the lessons of the last financial crisis may already be forgotten. The United States must make contingency plans before the dollar’s exorbitant privilege is visibly tattered and signs of hedging against it become clear. By that time, the damage may no longer be possible to contain.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

With just days to go until the U.S. midterm elections, many Europeans and Canadians are watching closely to see if Democrats will retake Congress and perhaps begin to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump for his final two years in office.

Canadians, who have been on the receiving end of some of Trump’s harshest trade actions, are so hungry for news about the U.S. midterms that they are searching for information at a higher rate than even Americans, according to Google search trends.

“Normal, average Canadians know so much more about the United States and care so much more about the United States,” said retired Royal Canadian Air Force Maj. Gen. Scott Clancy, a former director of operations for the North American Aerospace Defense Command. “Whereas Canada doesn’t even come into the daily [consideration] for the vast, vast majority of Americans in any given day.”

Europeans are also gripped by midterm fever. After Canada and the United States, midterm election information searches were the highest in Denmark, Qatar, and Norway—three countries that have also been rocked by Trump’s foreign-policy actions, from his aggressive claims on Greenland to the war against Iran.

Damian Murphy, the senior vice president for national security and international policy at the liberal Center for American Progress think tank, said that European officials he’s met with lately are “laser-focused on the midterms.” Murphy said he has been struck by the granular level of knowledge his European interlocutors have shown for the state of play of individual House races.

“What I’ve been telling them is that you shouldn’t have super high expectations for what any Congress can affirmatively do,” Murphy said. “In our system, the executive has a lot of power when it comes to the conduct of foreign policy. But what is important is the political message that it will send to the rest of the world: that the American people repudiate all of this—ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement], the Iran war, the treatment of allies.”

Other foreign observers have cautioned against high expectations of a U.S. reversion to pre-Trump foreign policies even if Democrats win control of Congress.

“Let us not overestimate the consequences of a defeat for the Trump administration in the midterm elections,” said former French Ambassador to the United States Gérard Araud in a recent post on X. “An American president holds considerable powers, particularly in foreign policy, and Trump can rely on the Supreme Court to bypass Congress.”

The experiences of Trump’s surprise 2016 and 2024 presidential election wins also continue to act as ballast against runaway hopes of a blue tidal wave.

“My philosophy of life is to have low expectations, and I apply that to the midterms as well. My mission is to stamp out any glimmer of hope of a return to normalcy after the midterms,” said one European diplomat, who requested anonymity to give an unvarnished take on the U.S. political situation.

One outcome with a strong chance of occurring in November, though, is a vote on impeaching U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over allegations of violating war powers and war crimes laws. A vote on the defense chief’s impeachment is likely to happen the week after the midterms.

Even if Republicans find the votes to protect Hegseth in the impeachment vote, a new impeachment inquiry may be launched in January if Democrats win control of the House, as is predicted.

Like the midterms, Canadians are likely to closely follow any impeachment process against Hegseth.

The former Fox News host “deeply offended” many Canadians this fall, Clancy said, when he separately appeared to disparage Canadian troop cadets and denigrated the contributions of NATO allied troops who joined the U.S.-led mission in Afghanistan.

“Personal friends of mine perished during that conflict,” Clancy said.

#6046. 5 things to watch for in Tuesday’s midterm elections

Midterm elections are almost always referendums on the party in power. That’s especially true this year, when President Donald Trump has repeatedly directed Republican voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.”

But Trump’s sagging poll numbers, driven by cost-of-living concerns and an unpopular war, have helped create a political environment that favors Democrats.

Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales projects Democrats could net four to six seats in the Senate, a scenario considered highly unlikely at the start of the cycle. To succeed, Democrats need to flip seats in several red-leaning states, among them Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. The party would also need to hold its own vulnerable seats in New Hampshire, Minnesota and Georgia.

On the House side, the question seems to be not whether Democrats will take the majority, but rather how big their margin will be. The party needs a net gain of three seats; Inside Elections projects Democrats could wind up winning 20 to 30 seats, a significant number of them in districts that voted for Trump by double digits two years ago.

Here are five things we’ll be watching for as the votes are tallied:

Republicans appeared to win the redistricting wars that defined much of the 2026 election cycle, especially after the Supreme Court weakened the Voting Rights Act, which led to new maps in several Southern states. Democrats gained favorable lines in California and Utah, but Republicans redrew more seats in their favor. The overall GOP effort put new districts on the board in places such as Florida and Louisiana but also sought to boost Republicans’ chances of ousting longtime targets, including Reps. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio and Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez of Texas.

While some redrawn districts are clear pickups, many redrawn seats are considered Toss-ups, forcing the GOP to deploy significant resources. Still, if Republicans make the gains they hoped to make in places such as Florida and Texas, it could go a long way in helping them either somehow keep the majority or narrow a Democratic one.

Historic gains among Latino voters helped Trump win the White House in 2024 and boosted GOP candidates in swing districts across the nation. Those victories also influenced Texas Republicans’ redraw of the state’s congressional map, betting that Latino voters would stick with the party. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

Across the South, the Trump-led redistricting push that dismantled House districts with sizable Black populations has fired up Black voters in states such as North Carolina and Louisiana. Black voters could also be key to determining the winner of Michigan’s hard-fought Senate race.

Democrats’ initial midterm target list, released in April 2025, included a few Republican incumbents who represented seats that Trump had carried by double digits the previous year. The number of “reach” battleground races in traditionally red terrain that fit that description has only grown since then. One of the biggest questions heading into election night is how many of those districts Democrats will be competitive in. Wins in those districts would translate into a larger Democratic majority or, at the very least, could help offset losses by Democratic incumbents in redrawn seats.

But flipping these districts would put a bull’s-eye on the Democratic winners, since their seats would likely rank among Republicans’ best pickup opportunities in 2028.

At the start of the midterm cycle, few could have predicted that the Senate battlefield would run through states that Trump carried by double digits in 2024. But concerns over rising prices driven by Trump’s tariff policy and the war in Iran have put several red-state seats in play. In the farm belt states of Iowa and Kansas, soaring diesel and fertilizer costs have GOP candidates on defense. In South Carolina, a divisive Republican primary and an untested first-time candidate have made the race unexpectedly competitive. And in Ohio, the return of a Democratic former senator, coupled with a national environment that is increasingly inhospitable to the GOP, suggests the state could shift from red to purple.

Recent surveys have shown Democrats with the advantage heading into Election Day and Trump’s job approval rating underwater, meaning more voters disapprove of the job he’s doing than approve. All signs point to Democrats retaking the House and potentially winning the Senate majority. That wouldn’t be unexpected — after all, the president’s party almost always loses seats in midterm elections. But polls have been wrong before. In August, some surveys predicted progressive Abdul El-Sayed would notch a double-digit win over Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, but El-Sayed wound up winning by less than a point. Throughout the campaign, Republicans have cautioned against reading too much into the polls, asserting that they typically undercount GOP voters.

#6045. How Russia Sees the World Now

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DMITRY ADAMSKY is Professor at Reichman University and an Associate with the Project on Managing the Atom at Harvard University. He is the author of The Russian Way of Deterrence: Strategic Culture, Coercion, and War.

The Kremlin’s New Mental Map Is Changing the War in Ukraine—and the Confrontation With the West

In 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine, the Kremlin’s strategic thinking was shaped around several core ideas. It viewed the United States as its principal geopolitical rival, an adversary that had encouraged Kyiv to impose strategic defeat on Moscow. It considered Europe and NATO largely as an extension of American power. And it saw nuclear muscle flexing as efficient means to exert coercive pressure.

Today, after nearly five years of war, and 22 months of the second Trump administration, the mental map guiding Russian strategy has changed. First, Russia now sees Europe, instead of the United States, as its principal geopolitical adversary, a shift that has driven Russia’s defense establishment to call for an approach known as “castling” to deal with the main threats. Related to this, Moscow now attributes new strategic agency to Europe itself because of the dramatic military modernization taking place in many European countries and the growing interest among some European leaders in developing or extending their own nuclear deterrent. A third shift concerns Russia’s theory of deterrence: Moscow’s traditional understanding of nuclear coercion is giving way to new thinking about nonnuclear strategic deterrence using advanced conventional weapons systems aimed at Europe.

These new lines of thought, which have gained prominence among influential defense intellectuals and policy experts close to the Kremlin over the past year do not need to be endorsed in formal security doctrine to matter. As the past decade has shown, ideas circulating within Russia’s national security establishment have shaped how officials frame problems, define options, and ultimately make major strategic choices. The three recent shifts in Russian strategic thinking will likely play an important part in how Moscow approaches any negotiation to end the war, as well as how it manages future escalation and competition with Europe and the United States.

As the Trump administration steps up its efforts to engage Moscow, it is now negotiating with a Russian leadership whose strategic mindset has evolved considerably since 2022. For the United States, understanding Russia’s new mental map will not only be crucial to any attempt to find an off-ramp with Moscow. It will also be essential to reducing the risk of inadvertent escalation between Russia and Europe and to ensuring strategic stability on the continent in the years to come.

One of the most notable trends in Russian strategic thought over the past year has been the emergence of the idea of “castling.” A term borrowed from chess, castling in geopolitics describes the repositioning of forces and resources to optimize a state’s strategic posture. Moscow’s defense experts have used the concept to describe a strategy for dealing with a new reality: for the first time since World War II, they have argued, Europe, rather than the United States, has become Russia’s principal geopolitical adversary. According to this view, European countries are now the principal source of Ukraine’s military capacity, political resolve, and strategic resilience; it is Europe and not the United States that has made Ukraine its proxy and is encouraging Kyiv to pursue Moscow’s strategic defeat.

As a consequence, Moscow must direct coercive pressure at Europe—its elites, its decision-making centers, and its critical infrastructure. By doing so, Russia can instill into Europe’s calculus what theorists in Moscow call a “deterring fear”: a European reluctance to antagonize Russia through further support to Ukraine. Such action, they argue, can also rebuild Russian credible deterrence for long-term competition with the West, which is now centered on Europe.

Castling does not imply a change in Russia’s overall objectives, which remain the same as those invoked by Russian President Vladimir Putin at the time of the 2022 invasion. These include banning NATO enlargement to Ukraine and other former Soviet republics; rolling back NATO’s eastern flank; and restricting NATO military exercises, as well as the conventional and nuclear deployments of NATO members, near Russian borders. The difference is that Russian coercion must now be aimed at Europe rather than the United States to achieve these objectives.

Along with this revised assessment of Europe, Russian strategists have interpreted the Trump administration’s own strategic stance as evidence that Asia has replaced Europe as the principal theater of U.S. strategic competition. They point to the administration’s reluctance to back Ukraine, its desire to terminate the war, and its continued overtures to the Kremlin. The administration’s decision in mid-October to provide sanctions relief to Russia and apply new pressure on Ukraine amplify this view in Moscow. Russian strategists also assume Washington seeks to solidify its control of the Western Hemisphere and views China, not Russia, as its primary long-term adversary.

Moscow believes that Washington is thus seeking to reduce its commitments in secondary theaters—particularly Europe and the Middle East—in order to concentrate political, military, and organizational resources on Beijing. As Russia sees it, the new American assertiveness in Venezuela, Cuba, and the Caribbean is unsurprising. By contrast, the current war in Iran—the biggest U.S. military engagement in recent years—has been read in Moscow as an unintended deviation from the new direction of U.S. policy, one that Washington seeks to correct as soon as possible. Whether this reading reflects actual American intentions matters less than that it has become a prevailing understanding in Moscow.

A related trend in Russian discourse is a growing fixation on what defense experts refer to as Europe’s “nuclear curiosity” and new military assertiveness near Russian borders. Specifically, Russian strategists have been concerned by the French and British governments’ modernization of their nuclear programs and apparent readiness to wield them more assertively. Moscow has also noted the prospect of French or British nuclear guarantees extending to European states and nonnuclear European capitals considering the development of nuclear options of their own.

Russian sources identify Germany, Poland, and the Nordic-Baltic states as “nuclear curious,” whether in pursuing nuclear-threshold status or seeking protection under French and British nuclear umbrellas. In this regard, comments by Polish officials in early 2026 expressing support for a Polish nuclear deterrent have been particularly noted. Russian strategists have also closely monitored discussions by Paris and London about offering extended deterrence to the continent as an alternative to the U.S. umbrella.

From Moscow’s perspective, any new attempt by a European state to become a nuclear power would cross a redline and could potentially create a casus belli. Moreover, Europe’s growing assertiveness on nuclear issues is happening in parallel with the deployment of conventional deep-strike precision weapons near Russian borders. For NATO, this more active European posture mitigates the risk of Washington shifting away from its European allies, but to Moscow it signals that Europe could potentially undertake strikes aimed at disarming Russia’s nuclear arsenal or decapitating its leadership.

To Russian analysts, these various developments also suggest Europe’s growing strategic autonomy from the United States. Traditionally, Moscow has viewed Europe largely as a “parking lot” for U.S. forces: a region of the world that is relevant but strategically subordinate to Washington. That assumption is changing. Along with the perception that Europe is now Russia’s principal geopolitical adversary, the continent’s increasing strategic autonomy, including on both nuclear and conventional issues, has become a crucial variable in Russia’s calculus. According to Moscow’s defense intellectuals, Russia may need to change its posture to contain this trend, including by seeking new tools to keep Europe at bay and to coerce it below the nuclear threshold.

To align with Russia’s new mental map, Russian defense intellectuals and military officers have been examining how to make Moscow’s coercive threats more effective. During the first years of the war, Russia’s nuclear muscle flexing and hybrid warfare failed to prevent Ukraine’s allies from funneling financial support, military aid, and targeting intelligence to Kyiv. This approach also failed to deter Ukraine’s land incursions into Russia and strikes on symbolic Russian targets and Russian strategic infrastructure, let alone compel Kyiv to surrender.

Today, NATO is preoccupied with Russia’s escalating cross-domain coercion, or what U.S. and European analysts call hybrid warfare. But that is only one part of the Russian approach. As Moscow concentrates on Europe as the new primary threat, it is also drawing on new tools of coercion that Russian experts call nonnuclear strategic deterrence. For Russian military authors, NNSD involves using advanced conventional capabilities, including precision-guided weapons, drones, ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic missile systems, as well as “weapons based on new physical principles”—a Russian catchall term for electromagnetic-pulse and high-power microwave weapons to deter and compel adversaries.

Conceptually, NNSD belongs to what Russian experts refer to as the “art of strategic gestures,” a euphemism for using, or threatening to use, nuclear and nonnuclear capabilities to deter and coerce an adversary. The concept is not new. Since the early years of this century, Russian strategists have tried to develop conventional alternatives to nuclear deterrence. But until the full-scale war in Ukraine began, in 2022, these ideas remained underdeveloped. NNSD has emerged from the lessons learned during the conflict.

From the outset of the war, Russia used tactical ballistics, cruise missiles, and hypersonic capabilities, which it has paired with drones and maneuver warfare. But even when coupled with the threat of nuclear coercion, this approach underdelivered, in the view of many Russian analysts. As a result, as the war has become entrenched, in particular since 2024, Moscow has shifted its focus to more advanced ballistic salvo waves, including strikes using Russia’s intermediate-range Oreshnik ballistic missile.

Drawing on this experience, Russian military theoreticians center NNSD on using massive, deep, precision strikes against the adversary’s critical military, political, and economic infrastructure. The strategy, they suggest, should be aimed not only at Ukraine but also at its European supporters. Although the exact contours of NNSD are still emerging, the concept appears to be more escalatory than the hybrid warfare and deniable asymmetric campaigns that Russia is currently pursuing in Europe.

This is more than a peripheral theoretical discussion. There are already indications that NNSD has gained traction among Russia’s senior military officers: for example, since 2025, the flagship journal of Russia’s general staff, Military Thought, has published several articles on the subject. All the branches of the Russian military are also developing their own versions of NNSD and are seeking to claim a comparative advantage in its execution. This interservice competition may increasingly normalize what constitutes acceptable coercion below the nuclear threshold and shape targeting priorities, as well as escalation management.

As the Kremlin sees it, the war in Ukraine began as an attempt to impel Europe to reshape its security architecture. Yet the strategic landscape confronting Moscow today may look even more threatening than the one it sought to change in 2022. Washington needs to recognize that the Kremlin regards Ukraine not as a discrete conflict but as part of a broader struggle over Europe’s strategic order. Any U.S.-led effort to broker an off-ramp in Ukraine will need to reckon with Moscow’s emerging castling logic and its mounting anxieties about Europe. A settlement that addresses the immediate battlefield while leaving Moscow’s wider frictions with Europe untouched is likely to provide only a temporary pause in this larger conflict. Washington needs to understand that Russia’s nonnuclear coercion has become a part of its ongoing deterrence strategy against Europe rather than simply a feature of the war itself.

Even if Moscow engages in negotiations to end the war, it is likely to continue using military coercion against Ukraine, as well as Europe. It will do so for several reasons: to align the terms of the settlement with Russian interests, to refine Russia’s emerging theory of nonnuclear strategic deterrence, and to force Europe to adopt a different security architecture. Russia may therefore undertake precision strikes on critical infrastructure, and even possible decapitation attempts, as well as calibrated attacks of varying intensity in Ukraine, alongside diplomatic engagement. By using such tactics, Moscow will be seeking not only to gain leverage in negotiations with Kyiv but also to restore its strategic deterrence with Europe. In response, Europe, doubting the credibility of the Trump administration’s commitments and seeking to demonstrate its own resolve, may decide to escalate.

Washington should thus be prepared for the possibility that stepped-up efforts to terminate the war may coincide with heightened security risks in Europe. Given that the dynamic between Europe and Russia is now characterized by pervasive mutual suspicion, conspiracy theories, and expectations of war, there is a growing danger of inadvertent escalation. Actions by either side that are intended as limited coercion, signaling, or leverage might be misread, thus triggering a self-reinforcing action-reaction cycle in which each side’s effort to restore deterrence instead erodes it. Paradoxically, this dynamic could emerge precisely at the moment when all sides—including the Kremlin—are seeking an off-ramp. Both Europe and Russia risk crossing a “culmination point of coercion,” beyond which any additional threats to use force, or its actual use, could expand the war further.

For Russia and Europe, then, the main challenge will be to bolster deterrence without crossing this tipping point. For Washington, the primary task is not only to mediate the substance of a deal but also to learn how to choreograph negotiations amid ongoing military action. It will be imperative for U.S. officials to anticipate coercive moves by all sides without mistaking them for a rejection of diplomacy—and without allowing them to derail negotiations. Washington will need to help both Europe and Russia contain their use of coercion before the security dilemma locks them into a dangerous escalatory spasm.
